content:
The Chair of the
Constitution Working Party, Councillor Yeates, presented
recommendations following the last meeting of the Constitution
Working Party held on 29 June 2026.
 
         
Councillor Yeates drew Members’ attention to a recommendation
at Minute 8 (Recommendations from the Planning Committee held on 19
May 2026) proposing amendments to the Planning Committee Protocol,
which had been considered by the Planning Committee at its meeting
held on 19 May 2026. The proposed changes were intended to improve
the Council’s handling of planning appeals, particularly
where Planning Committee decisions differed from Officer
recommendations.
 
Councillors were
being asked to approve introducing a new Paragraph 12.10 within
Part 12 of the Planning Protocol. Councillor Yeates confirmed that
the wording of the recommendation before Council differed slightly
from that previously presented to the Planning Committee as it had
been amended by the Constitution Working Party.  
 
The recommendation
was then seconded by Councillor Haywood.
 
The Chair invited
debate. During discussion, clarification was sought as to whether
confirmation had been received from the Monitoring Officer that the
amended recommendation did not need to go back to the Planning
Committee for further consideration. Members were advised that such
confirmation had been given and the recommendation could be
considered now.
 
         
There being no further questions or comments,
 
         
The Council
 
                   
RESOLVED
         
That the following
paragraph be inserted into the Planning Protocol part of the
Constitution (8.3, Section 3) as set out below:
 
Where the committee
determine an application and that decision is subsequently
appealed, Officers will liaise with members from the Committee
during those appeal proceedings. On the major appeals where there
may be a need to review or amend the council’s position
considering (for example) updated policies, consultee comments or
new documentation, the Group Head of Planning will agree to any
change to the council’s case in consultation with the Chair
or Vice-Chair of the Committee and the Council’s Monitoring
Officer.
 
 
 
 
 
         
The Chair then alerted Members to the next recommendation at Minute
10 (Changes to the Constitution – Officer Scheme of
Delegation) proposing amendments relating to the Officer Scheme of
Delegation, at Part 7, Management Structure, Delegations and
Authorities, Section 2, Officer Scheme of Management, relating to
Group Heads. The changes reflected interim management arrangements
within the Housing Directorate and formed pat of the Monitoring Officer’s
responsibility to keep the Constitution under review and to report
required amendments.
 
         
Councillor Yeates formally proposed the recommendation which was
then seconded by Councillor Haywood.
 
         
The Council
 
                   
RESOLVED
 
That the proposed
amendments set out within the Appendix to the report be
approved.
topline: The Council has decided to approve recommendations to amend the Planning Committee Protocol and Officer Scheme of Delegation within the Constitution.

content:
Councillor Lury, as Chair of the Policy & Resources
Committee, presented recommendations at Minute 79 from the meeting
of the Policy & Resources Committee held on 2 July 2026. The
recommendations related to the Local Authority Housing Fund 4
Funding. It was highlighted that the minutes from the Policy &
Resources Committee had been circulated separately to the meeting
and had been uploaded to the Full Council web page on 14 July 2026
and emailed to Councillors.
 
Councillor Lury then proposed the recommendations which were
then seconded by Councillor Tandy.
 
The
Chair invited debate and this saw support from Councillors as the
scheme would provide much needed accommodation for those that
needed it with the houses becoming part of the Council’s
general stock in the longer term. Some questions were asked
regarding the type of properties to be acquired, and it was
confirmed that once grant funding had been secured, the Council
would assess the housing market and purchase properties based on
availability and value for money. It was noted that properties
could include either new-build homes or existing properties already
on the market and that no decision had been made to prioritise one
type over the other.
 
Councillor Lury, as the proposer, added that educational
disadvantage among children and young people living in temporary
accommodation or bed and breakfast accommodation was significant.
He highlighted that providing suitable housing through the scheme
would deliver substantial benefits to affected families and
therefore represented a major advantage of the proposal.
 
The
Council
 
         
RESOLVED - That
 
(1) 
It includes this scheme within the Council’s capital
programme at a total cost of £7.465m funded from
£2.935m LAHF4 capital grant, £1.172m of Section 106
commuted sums and £3.358m through borrowing; and
 
(2) 
The new properties are let at affordable rents being 80% of market
rent (inclusive of Service Charges) in line with the viability
modelling for the scheme.
topline: The Council has decided to approve funding for the Local Authority Housing Fund 4 to provide much needed accommodation for those in need.

decision_maker: Policy and Resources Committee, Full Council
purpose:
The report has a dual purpose. Firstly, to
propose the extension and modification of the existing council
vision until April 2028 when Arun District Council ceases to be as
part of the local government organisation. Secondly, to update the
council on progress towards key objectives within each theme for
the year 2025-2026 of the current Vision document
content:
The Committee
considered a report presented by the Assistant Director of
Governance, People and Performance seeking a recommendation to Full
Council for adoption of the amended Council Vision
2022–2028.
 
         
Members were directed to the relevant sections of the report,
including the tracked changes version of the Vision and the
proposed final draft. It was explained that the amendments
represented a review and update of the existing Vision to reflect
the anticipated programme of local government reorganisation,
whilst remaining mindful of the Council’s available resources
and delivery capacity.
 
         
The Committee was advised that, in July 2025, the then Policy and
Finance Committee had agreed that officers should undertake a
review of the Vision in consultation with Group Leaders and
Committee Chairs, with changes limited to those considered
necessary to ensure the document remained relevant and
deliverable.
 
         
The Assistant Director of Governance, People & Performance
highlighted that the principal amendments included revisions to the
section relating to the Council’s approach to supporting
local communities and housing delivery, together with the
introduction of a new section intended to support implementation
and delivery of the Vision. Members were also advised of minor
additional amendments proposed following feedback received from
Group Leaders.
 
         
Councillor Walsh then proposed the recommendation which was
seconded by Councillor Hayward.
 
         
The Chair invited debate. This saw Councillors seeking
clarification as to whether adoption of the revised Vision would
provide officers with a clear strategic direction for future work.
The Assistant Director of Governance, People & Performance
confirmed that the document was intended to provide that strategic
framework and guide the Council’s future priorities and
activities.
 
          In
debate, one Councillor expressed concern that several issues
previously referenced in the Vision were either absent or had been
reduced in prominence. He cited arts and culture, beach access,
affordable housing, flooding, regeneration and energy efficiency as
examples. He questioned whether the revised document provided
sufficient ambition or strategic direction and indicated that he
would not support the recommendation.
 
         
The Chair responded by noting that all Group Leaders and Committee
Chairs had been invited to contribute to the review process and
observed that opportunities had been available for Members to
suggest amendments.
 
 
 
 
 
 
         
Another Councillor also expressed opposition to the revised Vision,
arguing that it lacked ambition and removed or diluted a number of previously stated objectives. He raised
concerns regarding references to healthcare provision, housing
standards, business support, skills development and wellbeing
initiatives, and requested that a recorded vote be taken on the
recommendation.
 
         
The Vice-Chair spoke in support of the revised Vision, noting that
it built upon a document originally developed in 2022 and should be
viewed as a living framework capable of adapting to changing
circumstances. He challenged several of the concerns raised during
debate, highlighting that a number of
objectives had been updated or replaced rather than removed. He
also noted that objectives relating to wellbeing, housing
improvements, regeneration and partnership working remained within
the Vision.
         
         
Another Councillor acknowledged the work undertaken but suggested
that the Council could adopt a more ambitious and proactive
approach within the document, particularly in relation to health
services and future priorities.
 
         
Referring to the Council’s achievements, the Chair
highlighted several major projects delivered or being progressed,
including the Littlehampton Seafront regeneration programme,
investment in the Alexandra Theatre, the development of new hotel
provision within the district and the Angmering Sports Hub,
considered earlier. The Chair suggested that these projects
demonstrated the Council’s commitment to delivering against
its strategic objectives.
 
         
With the agreement of the Committee, Councillor Goodheart addressed
the meeting as a non-committee member commenting that beach access
remained reflected within the Council’s work programme. He
also highlighted the importance of the district’s master
planning work and its role in shaping future development.
 
          In
summing up, Councillor Walsh as proposer of the recommendation,
stated that the Vision should be regarded as an evolving document
capable of responding to changing circumstances and priorities. He
supported the proposed amendments and commended the revised Vision
to the Committee.
 
         
Prior to the vote, Councillor Cooper made a personal explanation in
relation to comments made during the debate, clarifying that his
remarks regarding working with the NHS had been intended as a
general observation on the challenges of partnership working and
not as criticism of the work undertaken by Members involved in
health scrutiny activities.
 
          A
recorded vote had been requested earlier in debate. Those voting
for the recommendation were Councillors Butcher, Haywood, Lawrence,
Lury, Tandy and Walsh. Those voting against were Councillors Andy
Cooper, Greenway, Gunner and Pendleton. 
No Councillors abstained from voting.
         
         
The Committee
 
         
RECOMMENDS TO FULL COUNCIL
 
That the amended
Council Vision 2022 – 2028 be adopted.
topline: The Policy and Resources Committee has decided to recommend the adoption of the amended Council Vision 2022-2028, sparking debate among Councillors about the document's ambition and strategic direction.

decision_maker: Policy and Resources Committee, Full Council
purpose:
This report provides an update on the
Angmering sports hub project, and seeks approvals required to
implement the scheme, subject to funding.
The report will be considered in open business but is expected to
include an appendix which will contain exempt information as
defined in Paragraph 3 of Part 1 of Schedule 12A of the Local
Government Act 1972
content:
The
Principal Landscape and Project Officer presented this report
providing an update on the Angmering Sports Hub project and seeking
approval to increase the capital budget, undertake procurement
processes and award associated contracts. Members were advised that
Appendix B contained commercially sensitive information and would
only be considered in exempt business if required.
 
The
Principal Landscape and Projects Officer outlined progress made
since the previous update provided to the Committee in July 2025. A
planning application for the project had been submitted in October
2025 and approved in February 2026. Work was ongoing to discharge
the associated planning conditions, including a proposed
non-material amendment relating to the temporary relocation of the
cricket pitch during construction.
 
Members were advised that discussions continued with the housing
developer regarding the transfer of the site land. The developer
had also requested a temporary lease of part of the land to
facilitate completion of its housing development. Officers were
reviewing this proposal to ensure there would be no impact on
delivery of the cricket facilities.
 
The
Committee was advised of the successful award of £2 million
from the Football Foundation. Together with £3 million of
Section 106 funding and £1 million from the Community
Infrastructure Levy, this provided a total of £6 million in
identified funding for the project. Reference was made to the
business case summary attached at Appendix A, which outlined the
project’s benefits and risks. Members were advised that, in
addition to the sporting and community benefits, an initial social
cost-benefit analysis indicated that the project would provide
significant social value for the local community.
 
The
latest cost plan estimated the total project cost at £14
million, including allowances for risk, inflation and additional
expenditure already incurred. Officers explained that it remained
necessary to maintain contingency provisions until risks were
further reduced through the design process. Detailed financial
information was contained within the exempt appendix.
 
The
current focus was on procuring a design and build contractor
through Hampshire Procurement Services. Following appointment, the
successful contractor would undertake the detailed design stage
(RIBA Stage 4). Subject to the project remaining affordable at that
stage, it was proposed that the construction contract would be
awarded to the same contractor. A separate procurement exercise for
the 3G pitch supplier would be led by the Football
Foundation.
 
Councillor Walsh then proposed the recommendations, which were
seconded by Councillor Andy Cooper.
 
 
 
 
The
Chair thanked the Principal Landscape and Project Officer for her
presentation and invited questions and debate. Members sought
assurance regarding the proposed 3G pitch surface, noting concerns
raised elsewhere regarding microplastics and future regulatory
changes. Officers advised that these issues had been discussed with
the Football Foundation, which currently required projects to
proceed in accordance with existing specifications. However,
suppliers would be required to incorporate measures to minimise the
spread of infill materials, and any future opportunities to adopt
alternative solutions would be considered.
 
Members also sought an update on ecological matters,
particularly the impact on bats. Officers confirmed that the
necessary ecological assessments had been undertaken and that
appropriate mitigation measures, including adjustments to lighting
arrangements, had been agreed with specialist consultants and would
form part of the planning condition discharge process.
 
Questions were raised regarding site access arrangements.
Officers advised that the approved access point remained from
Arundel Road, opposite the school. Although alternative access
options via adjacent commercial land had been explored, project
timescales did not currently allow for this arrangement. However,
opportunities for such access remained possible in the
future.
 
Having discussed the report at length, Members highlighted the
importance of effective stakeholder communications as the project
progressed. Officers acknowledged this and confirmed that the
communication approach successfully used on other major projects
would be applied to the Sports Hub. Concerns were raised regarding
delays to the project programme when compared with the timetable
previously reported. Officers explained that revisions had arisen
from changes in project management personnel, the need to
coordinate work across a range of internal teams, and the
introduction of new procurement processes through Hampshire
Procurement Services. Members were advised that the project
remained on track to proceed to tender.
 
Clarification was also sought regarding the affordability review
referenced within the recommendations. The Section 151 Officer
explained that this was a standard provision included within
capital project reports and was intended to ensure that projects
remained financially viable. While decisions ultimately rested with
Members, the provision enabled the Section 151 Officer to advise
against proceeding should costs increase to an unaffordable
level.
 
In
debate, Members expressed strong support for the project,
recognising the significant benefits it would bring to Angmering
and the wider eastern part of the district. The Sports Hub was
described as an important investment in community wellbeing, sports
participation and public health, particularly given increasing
demand for modern sporting facilities. Members also noted that the
development would provide a lasting
legacy for the district.
 
The
Committee
 
         
RECOMMENDS TO FULL COUNCIL
 
(1) 
To increase the allocated budget in the
council’s capital programme for Angmering Sports Hub to
£14m, subject to an affordability review and agreed by the
council’s Section 151 Officer. This is to be funded through a
combination of S106/CIL contributions, capital grants, capital
receipts if any become available and through Council borrowing;
and
 
(2) 
Subject to Full Council approval of recommendation 1
and subject to a favourable affordability review agreed to by the
council’s Section 151 Officer, and subject to the bids being
returned within budget, authority is delegated to the Group Head of
Environment and Climate Change to:
 
a. Approve the procurement and
subsequent award of contract for project and cost management
services for RIBA Stages 5-6 (in accordance with 4.7 (i) of this report) within the total value of the
project costs; and
 
b. Approve the award of
contract for construction services for RIBA Stages 5-6 (in
accordance with 4.7 (ii) of this report), within the total value of
the project costs; and
 
c. Approve the carrying out of
a procurement process and subsequent award of contract for design
and construction of an artificial turf pitch with associated
fencing and lighting (in accordance with 4.7 (iv) of this report)
within the total value of the project costs.
topline: The Policy and Resources Committee has decided to increase the capital budget for the Angmering Sports Hub project and delegate authority for procurement and awarding of contracts.

purpose:
The report seeks approval from the Policy and
Resources Committee to adopt the Council’s new Resolution
Framework, which replaces the existing disciplinary, capability and
grievance procedures. The Resolution Framework introduces a modern,
values-led, person-centred approach focused on early and
constructive resolution of workplace concerns.
content:
In the absence of
the Head of People Services, the Organisational Development Partner
presented this report which sought the Committee’s approval
to adopt the Council’s new Resolution Framework replacing the
existing disciplinary, capability and grievance procedures.
 
         
Members were advised that the proposed framework introduced a
modern, values-led and person-centred approach, aligned with the
Council’s organisational values of trust, respect, kindness
and open communication. The framework placed greater emphasis on
early intervention, restorative practices and constructive
dialogue, with the aim of resolving concerns at the earliest
appropriate stage rather than relying primarily on formal
procedures.
 
         
The Committee was informed that the framework complied fully with
the ACAS Code of Practice and had been developed following
consultation with the recognised Trade Union, which was supportive
of the proposed approach.
 
         
Officers highlighted several anticipated organisational benefits,
including:
 

Improved working relationships
through earlier and more constructive conversations;

·       
Reduced escalation of workplace issues and lower costs associated
with formal procedures;

        Enhanced staff
wellbeing and psychological safety;

·       
        Increased
confidence among managers in addressing workplace concerns; and

        A more
transparent, fair and values-driven organisational culture.

 
         
Members noted that there were no significant financial implications
arising from the adoption of the framework, with the cost of
initial staff training to be met from the existing corporate
training budget.
 
         
The recommendations were then proposed by Councillor Walsh and
seconded by Councillor Haywood.
 
         
The Chair then invited debate. During the discussion, Members
welcomed the proposed approach, particularly the emphasis on the
early resolution of workplace issues and the move away from
traditional formal warning processes. The importance of recognising
opportunities for improvement and development within the workplace
were noted.
 
         
The Committee
 
                   
RESOLVED - To
 
(1) 
Approve the adoption of the Resolution Framework as the
Council’s primary approach for managing concerns, conflict,
conduct and capability issues relating to staff. 
 
(2) 
Approve the replacement of existing grievance, disciplinary and
capability procedures with the Resolution Framework for all
employees, except where separate statutory arrangements apply.
 
(3) 
Authorise the Assistant Director of Governance, People and
Performance and/or the Head of People Services to make any further
consequential changes to the Resolution Framework.
topline: The Policy and Resources Committee has decided to adopt a new Resolution Framework to improve workplace relationships and staff wellbeing.

decision_maker: Policy and Resources Committee, Full Council
purpose:
The Community Governance Review Working Party
was established by the Policy & Resources Committee in October
2025 to conduct a community governance review during 2026.
The Working Party met on 5 March and will be meeting on 16 June
2026 to consider and agree draft recommendations which will be
forwarded to the meeting of the Policy & Resources Committee on
2 July 2026
content:
The Committee
received the minutes from the meetings of the Community Governance
Review Working Party held on 5 March and 16 June 2026.
 
The Minutes from
the Working Party held on 16 June 2026, contained 7 recommendations
for the Committee to consider at Minute 15 (Current Representations
and Consideration and Agreement of Draft Recommendations). The
Chair reminded the Committee that any recommendations approved
would be forwarded to Full Council on 15 July 2026.
 
         
The recommendations were then proposed by Councillor Walsh and
seconded by Councillor Lawrence.
 
         
The Chair invited debate. The Committee considered the seven
recommendations presented within the minutes.
 
         
The Electoral Services Manager attended the meeting to provide
advice and answer Members’ questions. In response to a query
regarding future changes, she advised Members that the current
Community Governance Review process would continue until the parish
council elections in May 2027. Any further requests for changes by
parish councils would need to be considered through a separate
Community Governance Review process, with any future review
becoming a matter for the new unitary authority following local
government reorganisation.
 
         
Members commented positively on the work of the Working Party and
the collaborative approach taken throughout the review process,
noting that the recommendations broadly reflected the wishes of the
affected parish councils and communities.
 
         
During debate, a Councillor requested that recommendations 3 and 5
be voted on separately. Whilst supporting the remaining
recommendations, the Councillor expressed concern regarding the
removal of parish ward boundaries, stating that warding
arrangements could help ensure representation for distinct areas
within a parish and should not be removed solely for administrative
convenience or electoral considerations.
 
         
The Chair agreed that recommendations 3 and 5 would be considered
separately.
 
         
Councillor Lawrence, as seconder to the recommendations, spoke in
support of all seven recommendations noting that they represented
practical and common sense changes which
reflected local preferences.
 
         
Having then then voted on recommendations 1, 2, 4, 6 and 7, which
were approved unanimously, the Committee then undertook separate
votes on Recommendations 3 and 5.
 
         
The Committee
 
                   
RECOMMENDS TO FULL COUNCIL – That
 
(1) The recommendations in respect of the
Aldwick & Pagham Parish Council boundaries are approved in that
the boundary lines between Aldwick and Pagham Parish Councils are
amended slightly to allow 9 properties currently in the Aldwick
Parish to be included within the Pagham Parish along with the rest
of that housing development;
 
(2) The recommendations in respect of the
unparished areas in Arundel and Walberton are approved, this being
that the Arundel and Walberton Ward remains as it is and they do
not merge to form a new Parish Council or be combined with a
current council;
 
(3) The recommendations in respect of Bersted
Parish Council boundaries be approved this being that the number of
councillors for this parish decreases from 14 to 12 and that all
ward boundaries are removed so that the Parish Council is no longer
warded;
 
(4) The recommendations in respect of Bognor
Regis Town Council boundaries are approved being that the internal
boundaries are amended so that the Hatherleigh Ward be absorbed
into the Pevensey Ward;
 
(5) The recommendations for Walberton Parish
Council boundaries are approved in that the number of Councillors
increases from 9 to 12 and that approval is given to remove the
parish ward boundaries for the parish to enable equal
representation across the whole area;
 
(6) The recommendations for Yapton Parish Council boundaries are approved in
that the number of Parish Councillors increases from 10 to 12;
and
 
(7) The recommendations for Yapton and Felpham Parish Council boundaries are
approved in that the boundaries between Yapton and Felpham Parish Councils are amended so
that the Hoe Lane ward currently within the Yapton Parish Council boundary becomes part of
Felpham Parish Council.
topline: The Policy and Resources Committee has decided to approve recommendations for changes to various parish council boundaries and ward arrangements.

purpose:
The report provides a summary of the budget
process for 2027/28 for Members’ consideration and approval.
It is expected that the budget process will be supported by ad hoc
briefings to all Members, as and when necessary.
content:
The Committee
considered a report presented by the Director of Resources and
Section 151 Officer seeking approval of the budget-setting process
for the 2027/28 financial year.
 
Councillor Walsh
proposed the recommendation, which was seconded by Councillor
Butcher.
 
The Director of
Resources advised that the proposed process followed the approach
adopted in previous years. Members would receive a further update
to the Medium Term Financial Forecast before Christmas, after which
service committees would consider budget proposals relating to
their respective areas of responsibility. The Policy and Resources
Committee would then formulate the final budget proposals for
consideration by Council in February 2027.
 
Members were
directed to the timetable set out within the report, which
identified the key stages in the budget-setting process. Officers
also advised that, consistent with the arrangements introduced for
the previous budget cycle, Members would be able to develop and
submit budget proposals in advance of service committee
consideration. A detailed timetable and process for doing so would
be provided in September. It was noted that this approach had been
introduced following discussions at the Committee during the
previous year.
 
There being no
questions or debate,
 
The Committee.
 
                   
RESOLVED
 
To approve the budget
process for 2027/28 as outlined in the report.
topline: The Policy and Resources Committee has decided to approve the budget-setting process for the 2027/28 financial year.

content:
The Assistant
Director of Governance, People & Performance presented the
Council’s Annual Report on performance against the Council
Vision for the period 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026.
 
         
The Assistant Director of Law and Governance, People and
Performance advised Members of a correction within the published
report. Paragraph 1.2 should refer to Appendix A, commencing at
page 159, which contained the Council Vision aims, objectives and
measures update for 2025/26. Members were advised that the appendix
detailed performance against the agreed measures together with
commentary from the relevant service areas. It was further noted
that service teams had reviewed and updated the Vision outcomes and
proposed amendments to indicators for the period 2026–2028,
as set out in the appendices.
 
          In
response to questions regarding the Council’s objective to
support NHS provision, officers outlined examples of work
undertaken with health partners. Members were advised that officers
had been working with the University of Chichester and NHS partners
regarding dental provision within the district. It was also noted
that the Council had supported delivery of the new Croft medical
facility in Barnham, significantly increasing capacity for GP
services. In addition, planning officers had worked closely with
NHS representatives to encourage the use of Section 106 and
Community Infrastructure Levy funding to support healthcare
infrastructure.
 
          In
discussing the report, one Councillor welcomed the examples
provided but questioned why these achievements were not more
clearly reflected within the report. He also raised concerns
regarding progress against measures relating to the District Flood
Forum and beach access. Referring to the Flood Forum objective, he
noted that a report to Full Council had originally been anticipated
and questioned whether sufficient progress had been made. In
relation to beach access, he expressed concern regarding the pace
of delivery and whether the objective remained achievable within
the remaining lifespan of the Council.
 
         
The Chair responded that progress had been made in relation to
beach access, including the ordering of beach access buggies, and
emphasised that the Vision and associated measures remained subject
to review as circumstances changed. The Chair also noted that
climate adaptation issues raised by Members would continue to
receive consideration.
 
         
Another Councillor highlighted the role of opposition Members in
scrutinising Council performance and stated that Members should be
able to challenge the content of reports without having necessarily
contributed to their development. He argued that scrutiny formed an
important part of the Committee system and expressed concerns
regarding a number of measures and
priorities contained within the report.
 
 
 
         
References were made by one Councillor to further examples of
successful partnership working with the NHS, including the
establishment of a new NHS dental practice in Beach Road, which he
described as a significant addition to local healthcare
provision.
 
         
Further comments were made regarding the importance of effective
scrutiny and it was stated that
opposition Members had frequently provided challenge on reports
considered by committees. The delivery of the Premier Inn
development in Bognor Regis was welcomed but a question was asked
on the removal of the Public Art Strategy from the Council’s
priorities with clarification sought as to who had determined that
it was no longer a priority.
 
         
The Chair reminded Members that the report was presented for noting
rather than approval.
 
         
The Committee subsequently
 
(1) 
Noted the report at Appendix A which was
the fourth annual report, covering 2025-2026, on performance
against the agreed Vision for 2022-2026; and
 
(2) 
Noted the proposed Council Vision aims, objectives and measures for
2026–2028.

The Chair confirmed
that the minutes from the Housing and Wellbeing Committee meeting
held on 23 June 2026 had been circulated to Members as part of the
agenda supplement issued on 30 June 2026.
 
The Council has
been notified that it would receive £2.935 million of capital
funding through the Local Authority Housing Fund (LAHF) between
2026 and 2030 to support the acquisition of 18 homes. Of these, 10
would be used as temporary accommodation and 8 would be allocated
to the Afghan Resettlement Scheme, including four larger
four-bedroom properties.
 
These acquisitions
would provide high-quality homes that offered better value for
money than the current reliance on costly emergency accommodation.
The temporary accommodation properties would support households
presenting as homeless within the district, while the Afghan
Resettlement Scheme properties would accommodate families who
supported British forces in Afghanistan. It was noted that the
temporary accommodation funding was contingent upon participation
in the Afghan Resettlement element of the programme.
 
It was explained
that, although the programme spanned several years, the Council was
required to deliver 14 properties during 2026/27, comprising nine
temporary accommodation units and five Afghan resettlement homes,
as set out in the Officer report.
 
The total
acquisition cost was estimated at £7.465 million, funded
through:
 

£2.935 million LAHF capital
grant;
£1.172 million in Section 106
commuted sums; and
£3.358 million through
borrowing, supported by rental income from the properties.

 
Financial
modelling, including rental income, loan repayments and cash flow
projections, had been set out within Section 7.3 of the report. The
temporary accommodation properties were expected to generate
savings of approximately £260,000 per annum by reducing
reliance on emergency accommodation. Members were advised that
previous LAHF schemes had already contributed to a reduction in
expenditure on nightly paid accommodation during 2025/26.
 
The recommendations
in the report were then proposed by Councillor Walsh and seconded
by Councillor Butcher.
 
Before debate
commenced, the Chair highlighted that all Afghan families supported
through the scheme had been vetted by both the Ministry of Defence
and the Home Office and had a right to reside in the UK. Members
were reminded that participation in the Afghan Resettlement Scheme
was a condition of securing funding for the temporary accommodation
properties.
 
During discussion,
Members noted the positive financial and housing benefits of the
scheme, including its contribution to the Housing Revenue Account
and the reduction in expenditure on emergency accommodation.
Officers confirmed that the business case assumed a 40-year asset
life for the acquired properties.
 
Members also
discussed the Afghan Resettlement Scheme, noting the contribution
made by Afghan families who had supported British forces. Officers
clarified that households accommodated under the scheme were
granted tenancies in the same way as other Council tenants and were
not subject to refugee status conditions.
 
In summing up,
Members acknowledged both the practical benefits of increasing
temporary accommodation provision and the Council’s
commitment to supporting eligible Afghan families.
 
The Committee
 
         
RECOMMENDS TO FULL COUNCIL
 
(1) 
It includes this scheme within the Council’s capital
programme at a total cost of £7.465m funded from
£2.935m LAHF4 capital grant, £1.172m of Section 106
commuted sums and £3.358m through borrowing; and
 
(2)  
The new properties are let at affordable rents being 80% of market
rent (inclusive of Service Charges) in line with the viability
modelling for the scheme.
topline: The Council has decided to acquire 18 homes to support temporary accommodation and the Afghan Resettlement Scheme, funded through a mix of grants, commuted sums, and borrowing.

content:
The Assistant
Director for Governance, People & Performance presented for
approval the annual Calendar of Meetings for 2026/27 and confirmed
that this had been shared with Group Leaders and their Deputies and
Committee Chairs for comment prior to its publication.
 
         
Members were reminded that the meeting dates had been set in line
with the frequency previously approved by Council and that when
drafting the calendar, the Committee Services Manager had taken
several factors into account, to include avoiding political party
conference weeks in September and October 2026, avoiding the LGA
Conference in July 2026, minimising clashes with school holidays,
aligning meetings with Key Performance Indicator (KPI) reporting
cycles and ensuring dates sat suitably with financial deadlines,
particularly the budget setting timetables.
 
         
Councillor Lury then formally proposed the approval of the calendar
of meetings which was then seconded by Councillor Nash.
 
         
The Chair invited debate. One Councillor raised concerns regarding
the lengthy agendas experienced at recent Economy and Policy &
Resources Committee meetings. He noted that the proposed calendar
made no provision for additional meetings, despite these
significant workloads. He also highlighted that there would be a
three?month gap between Economy Committee meetings and nearly a
four?month gap between Policy & Resources meetings, from early
July to late October. He therefore sought reassurance that
additional meetings may be scheduled in due course.
 
In response, the
Chair confirmed that the matter had been raised and discussed at
the last meeting of the Policy & Resources Committee held on 12
March 2026 and had been noted in those minutes. The Constitution
Working Party (CWP) would be considering meeting frequency. While
the Chair could not confirm whether additional meeting dates would
be inserted into the gaps identified, this would be something that
the Working Party could review.
 
In responding, the
Assistant Director for Governance, People & Performance
reminded Councillors that extraordinary or additional meetings did
not necessarily require approval from (CWP) and could be scheduled
where needed. It was suggested that, given current workloads,
additional summer meetings, particularly for the Economy Committee,
may be necessary, even if not included in the standard annual
calendar. It was also explained that Chairs and members of the
relevant committees should work with lead officers and Committee
Services to review upcoming work programmes. This would enable
consideration of whether additional meetings were realistically
required and to schedule them as appropriate.
 
The Council
 
         
         
RESOLVED
 
         
         
That the Calendar of Meetings for 2026/27 be approved.
topline: The Full Council has decided to approve the Calendar of Meetings for 2026/27, despite concerns raised about gaps between meetings and the need for additional meetings to accommodate workloads.

content:
The Chair of the
Constitution Working Party, Councillor Yeates, presented
recommendations following the last meeting of the Constitution
Working Party held on 26 January 2026.
 
         
Councillor Yeates drew Members’ attention to a recommendation
at Minute 18 (Changes to the Constitution) which proposed to
address a gap in the Council’s employment rules. Following
the senior management restructure in 2025, two Assistant Director
posts were created, but the Constitution did not currently set out
the appointment and dismissal procedures for these roles.
Clarifying these arrangements was necessary to ensure sound
governance, transparency, and fairness.
 
The Constitution
Working Party had reviewed the matter, considering the structure of
the organisation and the differing status of the Assistant Director
roles. It was therefore recommended that Full Council approve the
proposed amendments to ensure that the Constitution accurately
reflected the current organisational structure and supported robust
employment practices.
 
Members were also
advised that further consequential updates were required elsewhere
in the Constitution to reflect recent changes to job titles
resulting from the restructure, such as the renaming of the
Director of Growth role to Deputy Chief Executive. Under Article 14
(Review and Revision of the Constitution), authority was delegated
to the Monitoring Officer, in consultation with the Chair of the
Constitution Working Party, to make such updates. These amendments
would be completed prior to publication of the next version of the
Constitution.
 
The recommendation
was then seconded by Councillor Haywood.
 
         
Following some debate, the Council
 
                   
RESOLVED
 
That the proposed
amendments to the Constitution, as set out in Appendices 1 and 2 of
the report be approved.
topline: The Council has decided to approve proposed amendments to address a gap in employment rules for Assistant Director roles

The Chief Executive
presented a report on the appointment of an Interim Assistant
Director of Governance, People and Performance, to be designated as
the Council’s statutory Monitoring Officer. Members were
advised that the current post holder, Mr Daniel Bainbridge, would
leave the Council on 6 April 2026, and the Council’s thanks
were placed on record for his service.
 
Members noted the
Council’s statutory duty under Section 5 of the Local
Government and Housing Act 1989 to appoint a Monitoring Officer.
Given the length and complexity of recruiting to the permanent
role, it was anticipated that the Council could otherwise be
without a post holder for up to six months. To ensure continuity
and statutory compliance, an interim appointment was therefore
required.
 
Following a
competitive recruitment process involving specialist agencies and
interviews conducted by the Chief Executive and the current
Monitoring Officer, Mr Sukdave Guman was identified as the
preferred candidate, bringing significant experience in governance,
standards, and organisational leadership.
 
Members were asked
to note the estimated cost of the interim arrangement for 2026/27
of £162,000, largely offset by savings from the vacant
permanent post budget of £123,000, with any remaining cost to
be managed through underspends or, if necessary, corporate
contingency. Alternative options, including a shared Monitoring
Officer arrangement, had been explored but were not feasible. The
interim appointment was therefore confirmed as the only viable and
legally compliant option.
         
         
Councillor Lury then proposed the recommendation set out in the
report which was seconded by Councillor Nash.
 
         
The Chair invited debate. In response to a point of clarification,
the Chief Executive confirmed that the estimated cost of
£162,000 referred to in the report was based on an estimated
six?month period of employment, calculated at the agreed agency
rate for the interim appointment. Clarification was also sought on
paragraph 3.1 of the report regarding the duration of the interim
appointment, querying whether the period of up to six months could
extend beyond this timeframe, particularly considering wider local
government reorganisation and its potential impact on recruitment.
The Chief Executive advised that six months represented an estimate
and that the duration could be shorter or longer, depending on the
timing of a successful permanent appointment. It was emphasised
that early engagement with recruitment agencies had been positive
and confidence was expressed that there would be a strong field of
candidates for the permanent role.
 
The council
 
         
 
 
 
         
         
RESOLVED
 
That it confirms
the appointment of Sukdave Ghuman to the post of Interim Assistant
Director of Governance, People & Performance (Monitoring
Officer) in accordance with the council’s constitution for a
period of up to six months or until such a time as the council
appoints to the permanent post of Assistant Director of Governance,
People & Performance.
topline: The Council has decided to appoint Sukdave Ghuman as the Interim Assistant Director of Governance, People & Performance (Monitoring Officer) to ensure continuity and statutory compliance.

out below:
 

CP21 (Percentage of non?emergency
repairs completed within 20 working days) – this had worsened
this quarter and needed further explanation.
CP42 (Overall tenant satisfaction)
as this showed a slight decline and little overall progress.

 
That Councillor
also noted expected improvement in household waste performance in
upcoming quarters. Finally, they highlighted the absence of any
KPIs related to climate change or sustainability, suggesting the
committee consider introducing such measures. The Chair agreed this
should be reviewed.
 
Other observations
made related to concerns regarding CP24 (household waste sent for
re-use, recycling and composting), noting that performance was
declining each quarter and that the explanation provided was
insufficient. Councillors doubted that the upcoming food?waste
rollout alone would significantly improve results and they
requested more emphasis on understanding why the council was
underperforming compared to other districts. There were Councillors
that argued that the upcoming new waste contract, starting in a
month, would be the key factor to watch, arguing that national
evidence showed food?waste collection typically led to substantial
increases in recycling rates. A noticeable improvement was
therefore expected within the first year.
 
         
The Committee
 
 
 
 
 
 
                   
RESOLVED – That it
 

(1) 
Approves that we no longer collect information for KPI CP36, the
number of new homes completed. Due to the uncertainty of the data
we are receiving for this KPI, it is recommended that we no longer
collect information as the data has little real time value. The
data is received from the Valuation Office Agency (VOA) who are
experiencing issues with their new system; and
 

(2) 
Approve the recommendation from the Housing & Wellbeing
Committee to approve the proposed increase in the target figure for
CP11 Number of Visits to Council Leisure Centres from the existing
fixed annual target of 956,650 to 1,580,000 in 2026/27 and
1,605,926 in 2027/28.
topline: The Policy and Resources Committee has decided to approve recommendations to stop collecting data for a specific KPI and increase the target number of visits to council leisure centres.

purpose:
This report provides an update on projects
within the Action Plan and an overview of the Council’s Scope
1, 2 and 3 emissions for the 2024-2025 financial year. This is in
line with the 2030 carbon neutral target.
content:
The Climate Change
and Sustainability Manager presented a report providing an update
on projects within the Action Plan and an overview of the
Council’s Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions for the 2024-2025
financial year.
 
The Committee was
reminded that the Climate Change and Sustainability Work Plan had
first been approved in February 2022 and this represented the
fourth update to Members. The plan supported the Council’s
2030 carbon neutral target and set out the full range of
sustainability actions being undertaken, reporting emissions across
all three scopes, these were:
 
Scope 1: Emissions from heating council
buildings and operating fleet vehicles
Scope 2: Emissions from purchased
electricity
Scope 3: Emissions from wider supply?chain and
operational activities, such as procured goods and services,
business travel, and staff commuting
 
It was noted that
Scope 3 accounted for 99% of the Council’s total emissions,
with the largest contributors identified in the report.
Particular reference was made to the
Combined Cleansing Contract, where Biffa would now provide contract
specific emissions reporting, had pledged a 2030 carbon?neutral
target, was transitioning fleet vehicles to lower carbon
alternatives, installing solar panels at its depot, and undertaking
regular engagement on sustainability.
 
Turning to the
Grounds Maintenance Contract, the Council’s fourth largest
supplier emitter, Members were advised that the contract now
contained emissions requirements, including commitments to
transition to electric equipment, undertake fleet reviews, maximise
opportunities towards net zero and produce a contract specific
action plan.
 
The Committee was
further informed that the Council was developing a Sustainable
Procurement Policy and was working with external consultants to
ensure a proportionate and effective approach, including deeper
engagement with key suppliers.
 
The recommendations
in the report were then proposed by Councillor Nash and seconded by
Councillor Walsh.
 
The Chair invited
debate. A member raised concerns regarding the balance and clarity
of the action plan. While acknowledging positive work, he
considered the Plan to be overly focused on mitigation and lacking
emphasis on climate adaptation, despite increasing local impacts
such as flooding, extreme rainfall, heatwaves, water scarcity, and
drought. He suggested that while the Council’s influence on
global emissions was limited, it had an important responsibility
for local resilience, which the plan did not address.
 
Concerns were also
raised regarding the clarity and quality of the actions listed
within the plan. Examples identified included:
 
·      
Action 17 - Green Flags – the action and aim was unclear,
only defining what a Green Flag was, rather than stating the
Council’s objective. Progress and impact were also considered
vague.
·      
Action 14 - Bersted Brooks – the action lacked clarity and
did not specify what the intended outcomes were. 
 
The Member also
highlighted the absence of Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and
measurable indicators, making it difficult for the Committee to
monitor progress or hold the Council to account. He further noted
the absence of any reference to agriculture and farming, despite
their known contribution to biodiversity and water quality issues,
as evidenced through the Flood Forum.
 
In response,
officers advised that the Council was working with West Sussex
County Council and other districts on a countywide climate
adaptation strategy, which would be incorporated into the Work Plan
once complete. They acknowledged the need to strengthen the
flooding related actions and confirmed they could work with
engineers to draft an additional action. Officers would also review
the clarity of actions, aim, progress and impact descriptions,
noting the challenge of summarising extensive work within an
already lengthy document. They confirmed that Member feedback would
be reflected in future iterations.
 
A further Member
challenged the suggestion that good progress was being made on
Scopes 1 and 2. He noted that earlier years’ data were not
comparable due to different methodologies and that since 2022/23
there had been no measurable reduction in the Council’s own
emissions. He expressed concern that this indicated limited impact
despite significant investment and suggested that the Council was
“wildly off” its net?zero trajectory. He questioned the
Council’s seriousness in delivering change, particularly
in light of actions lacking clear
targets and measurable outcomes. He also sought clarification on
the appointment date of the consultant responsible for reviewing
procurement processes and supplier emissions, and when tangible
outputs could be expected.
 
Officers explained
that reducing emissions from purchased goods and services was
inherently challenging because reporting lagged by a year, and
significant changes could not easily be made once contracts were
signed. They highlighted that embedding sustainability requirements
into major contracts represented important progress. Work on
sustainable procurement had accelerated in recent months, but due
to its complexity, particularly in ensuring fairness for SMEs,
external expertise had been required.
 
A Member expressed
concern that serious work on procurement had only begun recently,
despite suppliers being recognised as the Council’s largest
emissions source for several years. He questioned the
Council’s overall commitment to achieving net zero,
particularly in light of unchanged Scope
1 and 2 emissions over the last two years.
 
A question was
raised regarding the carbon reduction curve shown in the report,
specifically where the Council’s actual 2026 position sat
relative to the intended trajectory. Officers advised that the
curve represented the pathway that most local authorities had
planned to follow, but progress was currently constrained by high
costs, lack of external funding for building improvements, and the
wider challenges faced by all authorities, particularly in reducing
Scope 3 emissions.
 
Finally,
clarification was sought on whether the net?zero commitment within
the cleansing contract would be achieved through genuine emissions
reduction or through carbon offsetting, which a member described as
greenwashing. Officers advised that they would
confirm the specific wording via a written response
back.
 
Having considered
the report and provided observations to officers, the Committee
 
RESOLVED
 
That the challenges
identified in reducing emissions referred to within the report be
noted.
topline: The Policy and Resources Committee has decided to approve recommendations in the Council's Climate Change and Sustainability Work Plan, despite concerns raised by members about the plan's clarity and effectiveness.

purpose:
The report allows the Policy and Finance
Committee to consider and comment on the Council’s Capital
Strategy 2026/27 to 2030/31 before adoption by Full Council on 25
March 2025.
content:
The Group Head of
Financial Services presented the Capital Strategy for 2026/27 to
2030/31, updated in line with the CIPFA Prudential Code. The
strategy set out the principles that governed capital expenditure
and investment, ensuring alignment with service objectives,
consideration of value for money, affordability and sustainability,
and an assessment of risks and rewards linked to achieving priority
outcomes.
 
It was explained to
the Committee that the strategy did not make decisions on the
Council’s capital programme as those decisions continued to
be made by the relevant committees. Instead, the strategy provided
the framework that shaped capital investment decisions and
supported the development of capital budgets, ensuring the
programme aligned with the Council’s vision and maintained
financial sustainability.
 
The strategy linked
with key documents including Treasury Management, Annual
Investment, the HRA Business Plan, and Asset Management and
Property Investment strategies, promoting coordinated financial
planning.
 
The report also
updated the position on Capital Expenditure and Financing,
reflecting the latest estimates used in the budget approved at the
Special Meeting of the Council held on 25 February 2026. For
Treasury Management, it showed projected debt levels against the
Capital Financing Requirement to highlight over/under-borrowing.
This section outlined prudential indicators such as the operational
boundary and authorised limit for borrowing, consistent with the
Treasury Management and Annual Investment Strategies approved by
the Audit, Governance & Standards Committee at its meeting held
on 23 February 2026.
 
The recommendation
was then proposed by Councillor Walsh and seconded by Councillor
Butcher.
 
The Committee
 
         
RECOMMEND TO FULL COUNCIL
 
         
That the Capital Strategy 2026/27 to 2030/31 be adopted.
topline: The Policy and Resources Committee has decided to adopt the Capital Strategy for 2026/27 to 2030/31, shaping capital investment decisions and supporting financial sustainability.

content:
In the absence of
the Complaints Manager, the Assistant Director of Governance,
People & Performance presented a new Managing Unreasonable
Behaviour Policy, which combined and updated the former Customer of
Concern Protocol (2019) and the Unreasonable Behaviour Policy
(2023). This work followed a wider review of councillor and staff
safety measures, including updates to guidance, training, and
meeting procedures, alongside the readoption of the Feedback and
Complaints Policy.
 
The updated policy
responded to increasing instances of unreasonable, aggressive, or
threatening behaviour from a small minority of customers across
calls, emails, and face?to?face interactions, particularly
affecting high contact services such as Customer Services, Housing,
and Information Management.
 
The combined policy
offered a clearer, more transparent framework for managing such
behaviour, it set out clear expectations of acceptable conduct and
strengthened the Council’s ability to take swift action to
protect staff.
 
In presenting the
policy, the Assistant Director of Governance, People &
Performance confirmed his thanks to the Complaints Manager for her
work in merging and updating the two documents. 
 
The recommendation
in the report was then proposed by Councillor Walsh and seconded by
Councillor Lawrence.
 
Members were
invited to debate the updated Managing Unreasonable Behaviour
Policy. One member noted that the policy appeared focused on
office based staff, raising concerns
about how it would apply to outdoor workers and contractors such as
refuse collectors, who might experience harassment but be unable to
identify perpetrators. The Assistant Director of Governance, People
& Performance confirmed that the policy applied to all staff
and contractors and was based on managing behaviour and risk,
regardless of location.
 
A member then
expressed support for the policy’s intentions but could not
support it in its current form. They highlighted past Ombudsman
findings where the Council had wrongly used similar policies to
shut down legitimate complaints. They were concerned that examples
listed in the new policy, such as sending multiple emails,
repeating issues, or refusing decisions, could unfairly impact
residents who communicated differently, including those who were
neurodiverse or not confident with technology. They asked for the
policy wording to be reconsidered.
 
Another member
responded that these concerns were overstated. They argued the
examples were only indicators, not automatic triggers, and that
increasing unacceptable behaviour towards staff needed to be
addressed. They trusted officers and members to apply the policy
appropriately. A further member said they supported the policy but
felt unsure about including specific examples, as unreasonable
behaviour could depend on how it was experienced by the
recipient.
 
Others commented
that examples should remain, as they provided helpful
illustrations, and that the key issue was correct implementation
rather than wording. A question was raised about how decisions to
classify a customer as vexatious were scrutinised, and how the
policy ensured fairness and oversight rather than relying on the
judgement of a single officer.
 
In response, the
Assistant Director of Governance, People & Performance
explained that the new policy required senior level decisions and
replaced a cumbersome previous system. There would be a right of
appeal reviewed by a more senior officer, with the Ombudsman
providing external oversight. He stated that the examples were
based on those recognised by the Ombudsmen as legitimate signs of
unreasonable behaviour and that officers would continue to apply
professional judgement.
 
A final point was
made regarding the Equality Impact Assessment noting that the
policy was assessed as having a medium impact on people with
disabilities. It was felt that this highlighted that the assessment
itself acknowledged customers with disabilities may be more likely
to display behaviours that could lead to them being added to the
Customer Concern Register, which echoed some of the concerns raised
earlier in the debate. That Councillor shared a recent example from
the flooding response that aligned with his concerns. The member
stressed that without knowing someone’s disability or
communication barriers, there was a real risk of misinterpreting
their behaviour as unreasonable. They also expressed concern about
the policy’s reference to ending conversations early, as this
might prevent officers from identifying underlying disabilities.
Because of these issues, they felt that they could not support the
policy in its current form.
 
In response, the
Assistant Director of Governance, People & Performance
confirmed that the EIA appropriately identified areas of potential
disproportionate impact. He stressed that the policy required
officers to consider individual circumstances and make reasonable
adjustments, supported by increasing staff awareness through
neurodiversity and disability training. He highlighted that
flexibility was essential and that officers must understand the
reasons behind high contact levels and choose appropriate, tailored
responses. Some restrictions might not be suitable for certain
customers, and alternatives may be needed. He concluded that
although the policy acknowledged potential impacts, it contained
clear obligations to ensure reasonable adjustments were made to
avoid unfair outcomes.
 
The Chair closed
the debate by emphasising that the policy aimed to ensure fair
service delivery and committed the Council to proportional
responses and reasonable adjustments under the Equality Act 2010.
He acknowledged the concerns raised about complaint handling and
noted the role of the Ombudsman in ensuring accountability,
highlighting that the Council must continue improving in this
area.
 
The Committee
 
         
RESOLVED
 
That the Managing
Unreasonable Customers Behaviour Policy be approved.
topline: The Council has decided to approve a new policy to manage unreasonable behavior from customers, despite concerns about potential unfair impact on residents with disabilities.
