purpose:
This report considers the Council Budget for
2026/27 along with the associated statutory resolutions and
precepts from West Sussex County Council, the Sussex Police &
Crime Commissioner and Parish and Town Councils. The
recommendations made by the Policy & Finance Committee will be
forwarded onto a Special Meeting of the Council to be held on 25
February 2026.
content:
The Chair confirmed
that before inviting the Director of Resources and Section 151
Officer to present the budget report, he proposed to start with the
recommendations that had been submitted for this committee to
consider from each of the service committees.  Each of the
recommendations had been set out in the supplement pack circulated
to the meeting and uploaded to the web and emailed to Councillors
on 10 February 2026.  The Chair confirmed that he proposed to
take these recommendations on block. The recommendations were as
set out below and were from the:
 
·      
Housing & Wellbeing Committee – 20 January 2026 –
Minute 497 – Committee General Fund Revenue and Capital
Budgets 2026/27 – Page 2 of the supplement pack
·      
Housing & Wellbeing Committee – 20 January 2026 –
Minute 498 – Housing Revenue Account Budgets 2026/27 –
Pages 3 and 4 of the supplement pack
·      
Economy Committee – 22 January 2026 – Minute 510
– Committee Revenue and Capital Budgets 2026/27 – Pages
6 and 7 of the supplement pack
·      
Environment Committee – 29 January 2026 – Minute
523Committee Revenue and Capital Budgets 2026/27 – Page 8 of
the supplement pack
·      
Planning Policy Committee – 2 February 2026 – Minute
535 - Committee Revenue Budget 2026/27- Page 9 in the supplement
pack.
 
Having had these
recommendations proposed by Councillor Nash and seconded by
Councillor Walsh, the Committee
 
         
RESOLVED – That
 

(1)     The Revenue and Capital Budgets
for this Committee [the Economy Committee] be included in the
Council’s overall 2025/26 Revenue Budget;
 

(2)     The Revenue Budgets for this
Committee [the Planning Policy Committee] be included in the
Council’s overall 2025/26 Revenue Budget;  
 

(3)      The Revenue and Capital
Budgets for this Committee [the Environment Committee] be included
in the Council’s overall 2025/26 Revenue and Capital
budget;
 

(4)       The Revenue and
Capital Budgets for this Committee [the Housing & Wellbeing
Committee] be included in the Council’s overall 2025/26
Revenue Budget;
 
(5)  The
Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Budgets 2025/26 be included in the
overall 2025/26 budget; and
 
(6)  The
Revenue and Capital Budgets for this Committee (the Corporate
Support Committee) be included in the Council’s overall
2025/26 Revenue and Capital Budget.
 
          The Chair confirmed that
he would now focus on the whole budget for 2026/27. The Director of
Resources and Section 151 Officer presented his report setting out
the proposed General Fund, Housing Revenue Account (HRA), and
Capital Programme budgets for Arun District Council for the 2026/27
financial year, together with associated Council Tax proposals and
financial forecasts.
 
The Director of
Resources and S151 in advance of presenting his report confirmed
that Recommendation (f) regarding rent convergence was now
redundant because the Government had delayed implementation until
April 2027. This meant that it had no impact on the proposed
2026/27 budget and it should be withdrawn as a recommendation.
 
He explained that
the final Local Government Finance Settlement, received on 9
February, resulted in only marginal changes for the Council,
including a small £20,000 increase to the Homelessness
Prevention Grant. Although the Revenue Support Grant would reduce
by approximately £700,000, this would be fully offset by a
new support grant, leaving the Council’s overall position
unchanged.
 
The key highlights
of the budget were then explained to the Committee, as summarised
below:
 

The Fair Funding Review had been
delivered and provided a three year
settlement, subject to annual review.
The council was able to set a
balanced budget without using reserves due to a less severe funding
reduction than anticipated. The medium-term financial forecast
would be revised to reflect this and brought to the committee in
the summer.
Core Spending Power would still
decrease slightly, though less than initially reported because of
the settlement announced on 9 February 2026
The simplification of revenue grant
funding represented a major change with many grants being
consolidated into the Revenue Support Grant, simplifying the
funding structure. The changes had been outlined in the report at
Table 2 at Paragraph 4.5 of the report. Only a handful of grants
remained ring fenced, the Homelessness Prevention Grant was one of
those.
Council tax increase was proposed at
3% or £5 as allowed in the 2026/27 referendum principles.
Appendix 1 assumed an increase of £6.42 to £221.03 to
the Council Tax Band D.
The business rates pool following
the reset of the business rates and the fair funding review
outcome, would be disbanded for 2026/27.
This committee had considered all
the service committee’s revenue and capital budgets for
2026/27 and this committee was being
asked to consider an overall budget to recommend to a special
meeting of council on 25 February 2026. The total cost of the
service committee budget proposals had increased by £0.718m
to £29.593m. A summary table had been provided at paragraph
4.13 for members to refer to.
Corporate costs had increased by
£0.511m mainly because the council had added additional
contingency to cover unknown events and items that could not be
quantified such as the financial delivery of financial strategy
work streams, Arun Arts’ financial support and other events
unexpectedly arising such as large planning appeal fees
The proposed HRA budget was
presented with a forecast surplus and a proposed rent increase was
4.8%, with most tenants expected to be protected through Universal
Credit.
It was anticipated that the budget
would increase the council’s usable revenue reserves in
2026/27 by an estimated £577k. This would be impacted if the
proposals submitted by members set out in Paragraphs 4.33 and 4.38
were approved.

 
The Director of
Resources and S151 Officer confirmed that the council maintained a
healthy reserves position and reiterated that £10 million
remained an appropriate minimum reserves level. Capital programme
figures remained unchanged pending further cost information, but it
was hoped that some revenue reserves could be used to fund some of
the larger capital schemes such as the Angmering Sports Hub.
 
Finally,
members’ attention was drawn to the budget consultation
results that had been included in the report at Appendix 5. The
Director of Resources and S151 Officer confirmed that the
council’s budget estimates were robust, and the proposed
reserves were adequate for 2026/27.
 
Ahead of inviting a
proposer and seconder, the Monitoring Officer was asked how to
handle Recommendation F. The Monitoring Officer and Section 151
Officer agreed to confer and provide advice during the debate.
 
         
The recommendations were then proposed by Councillor Lury and
seconded by Councillor Nash.
 
         
The Chair thanked the Director of Resources and S151 Officer and
the Finance Team for their hard work which had been challenging,
given the late settlement received on 9 February 2026.
 
         
The Chair invited debate. A Member welcomed the report and
expressed strong support for the achievement of a balanced budget
with a surplus, describing it as a significant and positive outcome
for residents. The Member recorded his thanks to officers for their
work in delivering this position.
 
 
 
 
 
 
Attention was drawn
to the three member led proposals referenced in the report and the
value of the Business Support Grants was particularly highlighted
recognising their importance in assisting local businesses and
making effective use of the final year of the Business Rates Pool.
Also welcomed was the proposal to fund a beach access wheelchair,
noting that although the cost was modest, the initiative would make
a meaningful difference to residents with limited mobility.
 
Particular support was expressed for the proposal
relating to the Windmill Entertainment Centre due to its
long-standing role in providing theatre, performance and cinema in
Littlehampton. The historic lack of investment in the building was
emphasised with the proposed feasibility study being considered an
essential and a timely step in ensuring the Centre’s
continued viability and future improvement.
 
Debate concluded
with a member reaffirming their appreciation for the balanced
budget.
 
         
Councillor Nash, as seconder to the recommendations, confirmed that
he was pleased to second the recommendations and stated that he
could not recall a time when the authority had delivered a budget
in surplus. This was an achievement to be celebrated. While
recognising that such a position may not persist indefinitely,
Councillor Nash encouraged the committee to welcome the positive
outcome.
 
         
Councillor Lury, as proposer to the recommendations, commented that
the Council’s improving financial position demonstrated the
effectiveness of the administration’s financial strategy and
prudent management. It was noted that the authority was no longer
projecting a £5.2 million deficit, reflecting that
appropriate actions had been taken to stabilise the Council’s
finances ahead of local government reorganisation. On this basis,
the budget was commended to the committee to support.
 
         
The Committee
 
RECOMMEND TO THE
SPECIAL MEETING OF THE COUNCIL ON 25 FEBRUAY 2026
 
         
At 2.1
 
(a)The General
Fund budget as set out in Appendix 1 is approved;
 
(b) 
Arun’s Band D Council Tax for 2026/27 is set at
£221.04, an increase of 2.99% over 2026/27;
 
(c) 
Arun’s Council Tax Requirement for 2026/27, based on a Band D
Council Tax of £221.04, is set at £14.805 million, plus
parish precepts as demanded to be transferred to the General Fund
in accordance with statutory requirements;
 
(d)  The HRA
budget as set out in Appendix 2 is approved;
 
(e)  HRA
rents are increased by 4.8% to give an average rent of
£122.33 per week in line with the Government Rent Policy and
the Regulator of Social Housing’s Rent Standard;
 
(f) 
 For HRA rents, the council introduces rent flexibility levels
of 5% for general needs and 10% for sheltered accommodation for
re-lets to new tenants in social rented properties only, taking
into consideration local circumstances and affordability in line
with the rent standard;
 
(g)  When HRA
affordable rented properties are relet to new tenants, the
applicable rent is reset to the lower of 80% of market rent
(inclusive of Service Charges) or Local Housing Allowance with
effect from 6 April 2026 in line with government policy; 
 
(h)  That HRA
garage rents are increased by 4.8% to an average rent of
£16.84 per week (excluding VAT)
 
(i)    That all service charges
for sheltered and communal areas are reviewed annually to ensure
full cost recovery and that the charges are adjusted (either
increased or reduced) appropriately to reflect this
 
(j) The general
fund and HRA capital programme 2026-2031 as set out in Appendix 3
is approved.
 
The Council is
requested to note:
 
(k) That the
Director of Resources and Section 151 Officer, in consultation with
the Leader of the Council has approved a tax base of 66,978 for
2026/27;
 

(l)  That the HRA budget will provide a surplus of
£0.227m which will increase HRA forecast balances to
£1.433 m bringing them closer to the Council’s set
minimum balance of £2 million;
 
(m) That the
General Fund budget will increase the Council’s Usable
Revenue Reserves by £577,000 as set out in Appendix 4;
and
 
(n)  The
results and commentary of the public budget consultation process as
summarised in Appendix 5.
 
At
2.2
 
Having considered the budget proposals set out in paragraphs
4.35 to 4.37 of the report that they are recommended to Full
Council for inclusion in the 2026/27 revenue budget.
topline: The Policy and Resources Committee has decided to approve the budgets for various service committees, set the Council Tax for 2026/27, increase HRA rents, and approve the capital programme for 2026-2031.

purpose:
The accommodation
review business case examines the council’s office assets and
outlines options for the future of BRTH. The building is currently
underutilised and faces challenges related to running costs,
condition, accessibility, and privacy. 
These factors must be considered alongside service delivery needs,
strategic priorities, and feedback from members and the public. On
balance, the recommendation is to retain BRTH for the remainder of
Arun District Council’s tenure, allowing the successor
unitary council to determine its future accommodation requirements.
However, there has been a recent expression of interest from BRTC
to purchase the asset which it is proposed be explored and any
offer received considered in accordance with the CAT Policy.
content:
The accommodation
review business case examines the council’s office assets and
outlines options for the future of BRTH. The building is currently
underutilised and faces challenges related to running costs,
condition, accessibility, and privacy. 
These factors must be considered alongside service delivery needs,
strategic priorities, and feedback from members and the public. On
balance, the recommendation is to retain BRTH for the remainder of
Arun District Council’s tenure, allowing the successor
unitary council to determine its future accommodation requirements.
However, there has been a recent expression of interest from BRTC
to purchase the asset which it is proposed be explored and any
offer received considered in accordance with the CAT Policy.
 

(At the
commencement of this item, Councillors Nash and Oppler re-declared
their Personal Interests made at the start of the meeting).
 
The Project Manager
presented a joint report from the Deputy Chief Executive and the
Group Head of Technical Services outlining the findings of the
accommodation review for the Bognor Regis Town Hall. (BRTH). The
report presented a business case for the future of the asset, and
it invited the committee to agree a series of recommendations
relating to the continued provision of face?to?face customer
services in Bognor Regis, and the longer-term use of the Town Hall,
previously debated at the December meeting of the committee but
deferred pending this review.
 
The Project Manager
summarised the key elements of the report and the key findings from
the review as set out in the report covering heritage status,
staffing, maintenance, running costs, asset value and alternative
uses, required remodelling to the reception area, income potential
and public and member feedback.
 
It was reported
that, although disposal of the Town Hall provided the strongest
financial outcome, the report recommended retaining ownership for
now due to the strong public and member support for local in-person
services and the need to maintain flexibility for the incoming
unitary council to determine its longer?term accommodation
requirements.
 
Under this
recommended approach the Council proposed spending £74k on
essential maintenance and £73k on reception remodelling to
improve privacy and security allowing the continued delivery of
front?of?house services from the building. It was proposed to seek
to lease the second floor to reduce net running costs, with BRTC
being a potential tenant. The Town Council had also expressed
interest in purchasing the asset. Recommendation 2.4, if approved,
would provide the Town Council with a three
month window to submit a formal offer and business plan in
line with the Council’s Community Asset Transfer Policy. Any
such proposal would be brought back to the appropriate committee
once reviewed.
 
The recommendations
were then proposed by Councillor Walsh and seconded by Councillor
Lury.
 
The Chair invited
debate. A member thanked those who had supported the withdrawal of
the previous report and welcomed the revised report presented. They
asked numerous questions emphasising the importance of maintaining
frontline services at BRTH and urged officers not to enter new
leases with other organisations until discussions with BRTC had
concluded. The member supported the recommendations but did not
support recommendation 2.3, expressing concern about the proposed
£73,000 reception remodelling, which they considered
unnecessary. The member agreed that essential works should proceed,
but highlighted longstanding under maintenance of the building and
sought confirmation that any expenditure should not be added to a
future purchase price.
 
The member
questioned the indicative valuation of just over £1 million
and sought clarification on whether this figure included land
value, noting that the building’s listed status prevented
redevelopment and therefore limited land value. He referred to
potential valuation exemptions when disposing of assets to another
local authority and noted that protected tenancy rights would
further reduce open market value. He went on to state that an open
market sale would be unacceptable to the community. The member
concluded by thanking officers for the report and recommendations
and expressed hope that this would support constructive and
positive negotiations with BRTC.
 
Other councillors
speaking stated that they broadly supported the proposals, but also
shared concerns already raised regarding the level of expenditure
proposed for remodelling the building. They also expressed concern
about the projected ongoing annual running costs of approximately
£250,000 for a building with limited occupancy. An additional
concern was highlighted over reduced occupation of the building,
particularly the absence of staff on the second floor, which could
lead to accelerated deterioration due to reduced monitoring.
Reassurance was sought that appropriate maintenance oversight would
be maintained to prevent the building falling into worse condition
prior to any potential transfer.
 
Significant
concerns were raised in relation to recommendation 2.4. It was
noted that, while BRTC was being given a fixed three?month deadline
to submit a business plan and offer, the Council had only committed
to reporting back any offer at the earliest opportunity and so
greater clarity on this expected timeline was requested.
Clarification was also sought on what would be presented to members
at that stage. Would the committee receive a full range of options
or only a single proposal once officers had considered negotiations
to be concluded. The member expressed concern that officers and
members might take differing views on what should be considered by
the committee. The view was expressed that Arun was often regarded
as a challenging organisation for tenants and partners to negotiate
with and so it was hoped that the process with BRTC would be fair,
transparent, and free from unnecessary barriers.
 
The Group Head of
Technical Services was asked to respond to the points raised. He
confirmed that the upper floors of the Town Hall would continue to
be regularly monitored by Facilities and Estates staff once
vacated. Regarding recommendation 2.4, he explained that any
business plan and offer received from BRTC would be reported back
to members, with officers seeking clarification or undertaking
limited negotiation if required. The wording allowed for
exploratory work ahead of formal reporting due to uncertainty about
the level of detail that may be submitted.
 
In response to
earlier comments, the officer stated that while the condition
survey identified approximately £73,000 of required works,
this did not reflect significant neglect of the building. The
proposed reception improvements were informed by staff experience,
including incidents of violence and aggression and were the result
of a formal review undertaken by ROSPA to improve staff security
and privacy. It was explained that the market valuation had taken
account of the building’s condition. Members would ultimately
determine whether any offer from the Town Council was acceptable.
The Council had the legal ability to dispose of assets at less than
best consideration where there was a strong case for example for
social or community well being. Any
offer would need to align with requirements agreed by the
committee, such as the continuation of front?of?house services.
 
Following further
questions regarding the state of the building and the reception
remodelling, Officers explained that the works reflected RoSPA
safety recommendations, that the valuation included only minimal
curtilage, and that phased window and fabric repairs formed part of
the ten?year planned maintenance cost within the condition survey.
Assurance was given that no new leases would be entered into before
negotiations with BRTC.
 
The Chief Executive
explained that the Council’s Community Asset Transfer Policy
addressed many of the issues raised by members, including the
consideration of social value. The policy provided a clear
framework for assessing any proposal submitted by BRTC and enabled
the council to dispose of an asset at less than best consideration
where the required criteria were met. In relation to the proposed
reception alterations, the Chief Executive emphasised that the pre
Covid layout was no longer considered fit for purpose and she
referred to the RoSPA review that had identified necessary changes
to ensure staff safety, including the provision of interview rooms
with two exit points to allow staff to retreat to a secure area if
required. These recommendations had to be followed, and the council
had already worked to keep the associated costs as low as
possible.
 
A member expressed
concern that the Council had not been an effective custodian of the
Town Hall, citing issues such as the heating system in addition to
window replacements. They stressed the importance of raising
concerns early in the decision?making process to avoid difficulties
later. Clarification was sought on the process should no offer be
received from BRTC, noting that this was not explicitly addressed
in the recommendations. They also highlighted the need for timely
progress, referencing previous delays in other negotiations, and
emphasised the importance of swift decision?making given local
government reorganisation. The member stated their firm opposition
to Arun paying rent to BRTC for front?of?house services should the
building be transferred and asked for this position to be recorded.
Finally, the member asked whether any offer received by the
deadline of 12 May could be circulated immediately to all committee
members, noting that dual?hatted members serving on Bognor Regis
Town Council might otherwise become aware of the offer earlier than
others.
 
In response, the
Group Head of Technical Services clarified that, if no offer was
received from BRTC within the required timeframe and the
recommendations were approved, Arun would retain ownership of the
Town Hall, would continue delivering front?of?house services from
the building, and would proceed with the proposed reception
remodelling and essential maintenance works. Any offer submitted
under the Community Asset Transfer Policy would be brought to the
Economy Committee for decision, with officers undertaking initial
review and clarification before reporting.
The Chief Executive
advised that it would be highly unusual to circulate an offer to
members immediately upon receipt, as it would be necessary for them
to first assess it for accuracy, policy compliance and
completeness. Members were reminded that dual?hatted councillors
needed to carefully distinguish their roles and act solely in the
interests of Arun District Council when sitting on its committees.
The Monitoring Officer noted that while twin?hatted members may
become aware of information earlier, safeguards could be put in
place to ensure proper governance and to maintain fairness in the
decision?making process.
 
The Chair
emphasised the importance of ensuring members would be informed as
early as appropriate once officers had completed their review.
 
Having concluded
the debate, a request was made for recommendation 2.3 to be voted
on separately.
 
The Committee
 
                   
RESOLVED – To
 

(1)            
Retain in-person customer service from a fixed location in Bognor
Regis;
 

(2)            
Retain ownership of the Bognor Regis Town Hall (BRTH), and retain
the fixed in-person front of house (FOH) services within the
building for the remainder of Arun District Council’s tenure,
allowing the successor unitary council to determine its future
accommodation requirements, unless recommendation 4 (below) is
triggered;
 

(3)                
Undertake the reception remodelling and essential maintenance works
identified in the report under paragraphs 4.9 and 447; and
 

(4)                
That if a business plan and formal offer is received from BRTC in
accordance with the council’s Community Asset Transfer Policy
within three months of this resolution being passed, the option of
Community Asset Transfer of BRTH to BRTC is to be further explored
and reported back to the appropriate committee for consideration at
the earliest opportunity.
topline: The Policy and Resources Committee has decided to retain ownership of the Bognor Regis Town Hall, continue in-person services, and explore a potential transfer to a local council.

purpose:
This report is intended to seek agreement from
Full Council to ‘make’ (formally adopt) the
Middleton-On-Sea Neighbourhood Development Plan 2024-2041. The
Parish Council Neighbourhood Plan Group has prepared the
Middleton-On-Sea Neighbourhood Development Plan 2024-2041, which
was the subject of an independent examination in July and August
2025. The Examiner of this Plan concluded that subject to a series
of recommended modifications, the Middleton-On-Sea Neighbourhood
Development Plan meets all the necessary legal requirements and
should proceed to referendum. (Therefore, if the plan is successful
at referendum, then it should be made).

This ‘making’ of the plan will give it legal force and
it will form part of the statutory Development Plan for that area.
Consequently, decisions on planning applications in the
neighbourhood area will need to be made in accordance with the
Neighbourhood Development Plan or Order, unless material
considerations indicate otherwise
content:
The Chair of the
Planning Policy Committee, Councillor Yeates, presented this report
confirming that the Middleton-on-Sea Neighbourhood Development Plan
had passed examination and had received very positive endorsement
at referendum on 27 November 2025.
         
Councillor Yeates
outlined that she therefore proposed that the Middleton-on-Sea
Neighbourhood Development Plan 2024-2041 be ‘made to allow it
to become part of the Development Plan for the Arun District. This
recommendation was then seconded by Councillor Liry.
 
In inviting debate,
Councillor Haywood as Chair of Middleton-on-Sea Parish Council
confirmed her support and she urged all councillors to support the
recommendation. Councillor Haywood wished to have recorded her
thanks to officers and all members of Middleton-on-Sea Parish
Council and residents who were involved in what had been a
worthwhile but long and arduous process.
 
         
The council
 
                   
RESOLVED
 
That the
Middleton-on-Sea Neighbourhood Development Plan 2024-2041 be
‘made to allow it to become part of the Development Plan for
the Arun District.
topline: The Full Council has decided to make the Middleton-on-Sea Neighbourhood Development Plan 2024-2041 part of the Development Plan for the Arun District.

The Chair reported
one urgent item for consideration which was a report from the
Assistant Director of Governance, People & Performance
regarding the allocation of two remaining seats on the Audit,
Governance & Standards Committee. The report had been published
as a supplement on 6 January 2026.
 
In introducing the
report, the Assistant Director of Governance, People &
Performance reminded councillors that the matter had arisen from
the recent committee system review and the resulting
proportionality changes. He advised that officers had reviewed the
options in detail and concluded that the fairest approach was to
allocate the two seats to the political groups that were closest to
receiving an additional seat through rounding up of percentage
allocation figures and these were identified as the Conservative
Group and the Independent Group.
 
The recommendations
were proposed by Councillor Lury and seconded by Councillor
Nash.
         
During debate,
officers acknowledged minor typographical errors within the
appendix table, confirming that these would be corrected.
Councillor Gunner, as Leader of the Opposition, and affected by the
proposals raised concern about the lateness and urgency of the
report and questioned the work undertaken by officers since
publication of the agenda on 19 December 2025. He stated he had not
been consulted on the recommendations and considered the use of an
urgent report inappropriate, confirming he would not support the
recommendation.
 
In response,
Councillor Lury expressed surprise at this statement reminding the
councillor that the proposal aligned with the approach advocated at
a Group Leaders’ meeting to ensure that the Committee would
have a full complement of members ahead of its meeting on 23
February 2026.
         

         
The Council
 
                   
RESOLVED – That
 
(1) 
It approves the allocation of one unallocated set each on the
Audit, Governance & Standards Committee to the Conservative and
Independent Groups; and
 
(2)  
Subject to (1) above, it approves the appointments to the Audit,
Governance & Standards Committee for the remainder of the
municipal year.
topline: The UK council has decided to allocate two remaining seats on the Audit, Governance & Standards Committee to the Conservative and Independent Groups.

content:
The Chair of the
Policy & Resources Committee, Councillor Lury, presented the
minutes following the meeting of the Policy & Resources
Committee held on 11 December 2025.
 
         
Councillor Lury referred Members to the first of a series of
recommendations at Minute 434 (Community Governance Reviews within
the Arun District) which he duly proposed. The recommendation was
then seconded by Councillor Nash.
 
         
The Council
 
                   
RESOLVED
 
That the draft
terms of reference for the Community Governance Review programme as
set out in Appendix 1 is approved. 
 
         
Councillor Lury then drew Members’ attention to the next
recommendation at Minute 441 (Items Put Forward from Service
Committees – Housing & Wellbeing Committee – 25
November 2025 – Local Council Tax Reduction Scheme) which was
asking council to approve that the Council Tax Reduction Scheme for
2026/27 be implemented at a cost of £30,548 per annum.
Councillor Lury then formally proposed this recommendation which
was seconded by Councillor Nash.
 
The Chair invited
debate. There were councillors who spoke in strong support for the
recommendation as they were delighted to see that veterans were to
be included in the scheme and that it would assist those who were
most in need of help. There was one councillor who confirmed that
although he fully supported the principle behind what was proposed,
he could not support the recommendation without a more robust and
regular review mechanism in place to enhance enforcement. It was
that councillor’s view that straightforward improvements
should be implemented such as scheduled, systematic checks to
strengthen the control environment and reduce the risk of
fraudulent or improper claims. Until such measures were
implemented, he felt that he could not endorse the proposal,
despite agreeing with its underlying aims.
 
Other councillors
spoke expressing that any application for a grant or funding scheme
had the potential to be misused and to respond to any such risk
strong enforcement was the response, rather than questioning the
value of the scheme itself. The council’s new partnership
with Oxford Investigation Services had strengthened focus on fraud
detection and excellent feedback had already been received on this
work.
 
Councillor Nash,
as seconder, responded stating that the scheme was a well?designed
and well?structured scheme. He acknowledged the concerns raised
about fraud but confirmed that the controls and measures in place
were solid, and that the Council remained fully on top of the
issue.
 
 
Councillor Lury, as
proposer, stated that he agreed with the views expressed that
veterans deserved the council’s attention and recognition for
their service. He acknowledged the concerns raised but emphasised
that the partnership with Oxford meant that the council could be
confident in their expertise. He added that a certain level of
attempted fraud was inevitable in any claims process, but
appropriate systems were in place to manage and mitigate this.
 
         
The council
 
                   
RESOLVED
 
That the Council
Tax Reduction Scheme for 2026/27 be implemented at a cost of
£30,548 per annum.
 
Prior to inviting
Councillor Lury to present the next set of recommendations at
Minute 445 (Request for Financial Support for the Operation of the
Alexandra Theatre), the Chair confirmed that it would be necessary
to move into Exempt business to consider this item.
 
EXEMPT
INFORMATION
 
Having been
proposed by Councillor Tandy and seconded by Councillor Long, the
council
 
RESOLVED
 
That under Section
100A(4) of the Local Government Act 1972, the public and accredited
representatives of newspaper be excluded from the meeting for the
following item of business o the
grounds that it may involve the likely disclosure of exempt
information as defined in Part 3 of Scheule 12A of the Act by
virtue of the paragraph specified against the item.
 
MINUTE 445 FROM THE
POLICY & RESOURCES COMMITTEE HELD ON 11 DECEMBER 2025 (REQUEST
FOR FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR THE OPERATION OF THE ALEXANDRA THEATRE
– EXEMPT – PART 3 –
 
(Prior to the
consideration of this item, Councillor Woodman, having declared her
prejudicial interest at the start of the meeting, left the meeting
for this item).
 
Councillor Lury
then presented the recommendations at Minute 445 (Request for
Financial Support for the Operation of the Alexandra Theatre). In
proposing the recommendations, Councillor Lury confirmed that he
wished to make an amendment to Recommendation 3 as set out below,
with additional wording shown in bold:
 
 
3.    
That the council enters into a new lease
with Arun Arts for the operation of the theatre based on the draft
Heads of Terms set out in this report; and an updated business
plan with cash- flow projections for at least the next 3 years
should be provided.
 
The
recommendations to include the amendment to Recommendation 3, were
then seconded by Councillor Nash.
 
The Chair then
called a short adjournment for 5 minutes.
 
Having resumed the
meeting, the chair invited debate on the amendment.
 
Several
councillors spoke in support of the amendment stressing the need to
ensure a successful launch and sustainable operation of the new
theatre given the significant public investment to date. They noted
concerns that, without appropriate support, the operator having
been inactive for some time might struggle to deliver an effective
opening programme. Members highlighted that the partnership
arrangements outlined in the report would provide necessary
stability, strengthen organisational capacity, and help secure
long?term community benefits.
 
          A
range of concerns were raised given the potential financial
commitment and many questions asked regarding the proposed support
highlighting the need for strengthened governance and oversight.
Some councillors expressed disappointment regarding the proposed
amendment, noting that no explanation had been provided to members
about its purpose or how it aligned with the wider recommendations.
In view of this, there were members confirming that they could not
support it. 
 
Other councillors
highlighted that the theatre was a central component of the
district’s Cultural Strategy and played an important role in
diversifying the local economy, creating alternative employment
opportunities which would expand educational opportunities for
young people. They stated that culture had repeatedly been
identified as a key driver in these areas, making it essential that
the project succeeded.
 
A councillor
advised that, having listened to the debate, they did not believe
the Council had sufficient information to reach a conclusive
decision. That councillor felt that the report did not present a
clear or robust way forward and that proceeding based on the
current information would be unwise. Councillor Bower therefore
proposed that the item be deferred to allow the issues to be
reconsidered and a fully developed proposal to be brought back to
Council, noting that a special meeting could be arranged if
required.
 
Councillor Bence
seconded this amendment to defer.
 
Following further
discussion and having heard from the proposer and seconder of the
amendment, a vote was undertaken on the amendment to Recommendation
(3), this was declared CARRIED.
 
The Chair confirmed
that he would now invite debate on the amendment to defer.
 
         
Those speaking against stated that it would be inappropriate at
this stage given the investment already made and the need to
commence programming work for the theatre. A deferral at this stage
would risk the planned opening and theatre programming. 
 
         
Those speaking in support of a deferral stated that additional
information and cross?party discussion was needed before
considering the finances involved and based on the limited
information available.
 
         
Having heard from the proposer and seconder of the amendment to
defer, a vote was taken and the amendment was declared NOT
CARRIED.
 
         
The Chair returned to the substantive recommendations as
amended.
 
         
Having heard from the proposer and seconder to the recommendations,
the chair confirmed that as a recorded vote had been requested,
this would be undertaken now.
 
Those voting for
the recommendations were Councillors Ayling, Batley, Birch,
Blanchard-Cooper, Butcher, Goodheart, Hamilton, Haywood, Jones,
Lawrence, Long, Lury, McDougall, Nash, Needs, Northeast,
O’Neill, Oppler, Stanley, Wallsgrove, Walsh, Wiltshire, Mrs
Worne, Miss Worne and Yeates. (25). Those voting against were
Councillors Bence, Bicknell, Mrs Bower, Bower, Cooper, Mrs Cooper,
Edwards, Elkins, English, Greenway, Gunner, Harty, Kelly, Madeley,
McAuliffe, Patel, Pinnelli, Purser, and Turner (19). Councillor
Tandy abstained from voting,
 
The council
 
         
         
RESOLVED – That
 

(1)            
Up to £50k in 25/26 to facilitate technical support during
the construction phase.
 

(2).     To provide financial support to the
operators of the Alexandra Theatre in the following three years as
follows subject to conditions.
 
YEAR 0 (Apr 26 – Mar
27) £250,000.00
YEAR 1 (Apr 27 – Mar
28) £170,000.00
YEAR 2 (Apr 28 – Mar
29) £140,000.00
 

(3)     The council enters
into a new lease with Arun Arts for the operation of the
theatre based on the draft Heads of Terms set out in this report;
and an updated business plan with cash- flow projections for at
least the next 3 years should be provided
 

(4)    That the Group Head of Technical
Services and the Director of Resources & Section 151 Officer be
delegated to agree the final wording of financial support
conditions and the lease Heads of Terms in accordance with any
legal and procurement advice provided. However, the preference is
for Year 0 financing of Arun Arts (£250,000) to be in the
form of a grant, subject to further appropriate legal and financial
advice.
 
The Chair announced
that the meeting had re?entered public session.
topline: The Full Council has decided to approve the Community Governance Review program and implement the Council Tax Reduction Scheme for 2026/27, despite concerns about fraud and financial support for the Alexandra Theatre.

The committee
received a report from the Assistant Director of Governance, People
& Performance summarising the results of the Arun District
Council Residents’ Satisfaction Survey 2025.
 
It was explained
that the survey was historically undertaken annually and had been
carried out biannually since 2023. The 2025 survey had been
undertaken in April to May 2025 reflecting on services delivered
during 2024/25. The report presented the headline results,
comparisons with previous surveys and included a commentary
responding to the results captured from the survey provided by the
Senior Leadership Team.
 
The survey formed
part of the council’s wider performance framework,
complimenting quarterly KPI reporting and annual Vison performance
reporting and provided insight into residents’ perception of
the council, its services and the wider district. A summary of the
survey responses had been set out in the report. 
 
It was being
recommended by officers that the 2025 survey should be the final
survey undertaken by the council due to (LGR).
 
The recommendations
in the report were then proposed by Councillor Walsh and were
seconded by Councillor Nash.
 
The chair invited
questions and debate. Mixed views were expressed over the proposal
to not rerun the survey in 2027 due to LGR. Many councillors felt
that there were benefits in conducting a last review for the new
council to respond to and to have a more up to date appreciation of
how residents felt about their district.
 
The Chief Executive
confirmed that she had canvassed all other West Sussex CEOs, and it
had been confirmed that no other West Sussex councils would be
undertaking similar surveys between now and vesting day, the
decision to not rerun the survey had not been taken lightly with
work continuing to be undertaken to assess the council’s
performance via KPIs.
 
Turning to the
survey results, there were some negative trends that some members
felt could not be ignored. The public had indicated their
dissatisfaction over various issues but the most startling theme
coming out of the survey was the fact that distinct geographic
variations continued to persist confirming that those living in the
west of the district were far less appreciative of the services
being provided in their area compared to those residing in the east
or the downland areas. It was hoped that the development of the new
street cleansing KPI would assist in reducing such
variations.  Members felt strongly that
this was something that the council should take notice of and had
raised before when the last survey results had been debated. There
was a lot to take away from the survey results for the council to
improve on.
 
 
 
The chair
highlighted that with many of the issues highlighted, these were
problem behaviours that were not the responsibility of the council
and were issues that the council could not control. Action Groups
had been set up in Bognor Regis and Littlehampton to assist in
tackling the problems listed and so work was progressing in both
towns.
 
The committee
 
         
RESOLVED – That
 
(1) 
Having reviewed the survey that its contents be noted; and
 
(2)  
To agree that the survey in 2025 be the final survey to be carried
out on behalf of Arun District Council, due to the timing of the
Local Government Reorganisation.
topline: The Policy and Resources Committee has decided to make the 2025 Arun District Council Residents' Satisfaction Survey the final one due to Local Government Reorganisation.

purpose:
A decision is required on the future delivery
model for in-person customer service within the district. The
options are to continue providing the service from a fixed location
in Bognor Regis, or to change to a model that maintains in-person
customer service at Arun Civic Centre while enhancing provision
through an outreach service at additional venues across the
district.
content:
The Project Manager
presented a joint report from the Deputy Chief Executive and the
Group Head of Technical Services to the committee. It was explained
that this report formed part of the ongoing accommodation review
which sought to identify opportunities to achieve savings and
increased revenue generation. The report outlined the
council’s financial and customer service strategies which
aimed to improve efficiency, promote digital self-service and
support vulnerable residents.
 
The purpose of the
report was to seek a decision on whether to retain fixed in-person
customer service provision in Bognor Regis or to remove the service
and replace it with enhanced outreach provision. Outreach would
involve delivering services within the community at various
locations on set days.
 
The current
front-of-house service at Bognor Regis Town Hall provided general
customer services, housing and rough sleeper initiative support,
emergency accommodation assistance, parking services’
support, and public access to land charges. Usage data from January
to September indicated over 100,000 contacts via phone and online
channels compared to approximately 16,000 in-person visits, of
which just under 5,000 were at Bognor Regis Town Hall. Digital
uptake continued to grow.
 
Consultation
undertaken between 20 October and 10 November resulted in 275
responses, including 42 paper submissions. Financial analysis
showed that removing the front-of-house service would result in
annual running costs of £76,500 for outreach and associated
services, offset by £33,500 potential income from leasing
reception space, giving a net cost of £43,000 and a net
annual saving of £14,500. One-off costs for remodelling or
potential relocation would be considered at the committee’s
next meeting on 12 February 2026.
 
         
Having considered the consultation feedback and the modest cost
saving, the Corporate Leadership Team recommended retaining a fixed
in-person customer service provision in Bognor Regis. This option
aligned with social responsibility, public demand, and the
Council’s vision, while supporting vulnerable residents. If
retained, the specific location would be reviewed as part of the
further report to be presented to the committee in February 2026
regarding the future of Bognor Regis Town Hall.
 
         
Councillor Walsh then proposed the recommendation which was
seconded by Councillor Lawrence.
 
         
The chair then invited debate. Councillor Walsh addressed the
Committee emphasising that the Council was a public service
organisation, customer-focused, and should respond to clear and
comprehensive feedback from the public. His support for the
recommendation was based on two key reasons. Firstly, 77% of
respondents stated that in-person service support was extremely
important and secondly, while digital and telephone services were
available, the former was not universally accessible or sufficient.
He highlighted that this was demonstrably true, as many older
residents, and some younger residents with learning difficulties,
found it difficult to use digital or telephone services.
Additionally, some residents could not travel to Littlehampton (the
Civic Centre), which was understandable.
 
Councillor Walsh
therefore proposed an amendment to the recommendation which is set
out below with additions added using bold:
 
Agree to retain
in-person customer services from a fixed location in Bognor Regis
preferably at Bognor Regis Town Hall
 
The amendment was
seconded by Councillor Lawrence.
 
Councillor Walsh
further clarified that the Committee was not taking a final
decision at this meeting, as it had been confirmed that a final
decision would be made on 12 February 2026. However, he considered
it important to provide a steer on the committee’s
intentions. He noted that Bognor Regis Town Hall was centrally
located, near bus routes, was well known, and currently served as
the main point of contact. He concluded that continuing this
arrangement would be sensible. He acknowledged that ownership of
the Town Hall was a separate matter to be discussed later.
 
         
The chair then invited debate on the amendment. Many councillors
spoke in support of it. This was because the consultation
undertaken confirmed overwhelming support for retaining customer
services in the Town and that this should be the Bognor Regis Town
Hall. It was accepted that a report confirming the future of the
Town Hall would be presented to the committee in February and so
the committee felt that providing a clear steer now would assist
officers in compiling the report.
 
         
Other councillors spoke against the amendment and referred to the
petition that had been submitted and debated at Full Council about
saving the Bognor Regis Town Hall in January 2023. In response, the
council had given a solid commitment to preserve customer services
at the Town Hall, and it was strongly felt that this commitment
should not change. There was much emotional attachment to the Town
Hall, but equally there were sound practical reasons as to why the
Town Hall should continue to be used in the future.  Some councillors stated that they could not
understand the need for the amendment at this time and in advance
of receiving the further report in February 2026.
 
         
Debate then turned to members questioning why this report was being
considered now and not at the same time as the other report on the
future of the Bognor Regis Town Hall.
 
Having undertaken a
vote on the amendment, this was NOT CARRIED.
 
The chair then
returned to the substantive recommendation and invited debate.
 
 
 
 
Councillor Gunner
confirmed that he supported the sentiment of the amendment but
stated that the easiest solution was to defer the item until the
report on the future of the Bognor Regis Town Hall was presented to
committee on 12 February 2026, the two items could then be
considered together. He confirmed that he wished to propose that
this item be deferred as an amendment, this is set out below.
 
To defer this item
to the 12 February 2026 meeting of this committee so that it can be
considered with the item on the future of the Bognor Regis Town
Hall
 
Councillor Alison
Cooper seconded this amendment.
 
The chair invited
debate on the second amendment.  The
committee fully supported the deferral so that the future of
customer services in Bognor Regis could be considered at the same
time as the future of the Bognor Regis Town Hall. Those speaking in
support of this amendment reiterated the importance of retaining
customer services at this location and until LGR had taken place as
this was the clear wish of the public.
 
         
Following further debate, a vote on the amendment was then
undertaken and it was declared CARRIED.
 
         
The Committee
 
         
         
RESOLVED
 
To defer this item
to the 12 February 2026 meeting of this committee so that it can be
considered with the item on the future of the Bognor Regis Town
Hall.
topline: The Policy and Resources Committee has decided to defer the decision on retaining in-person customer service provision in Bognor Regis to align it with the future of the Bognor Regis Town Hall.

purpose:

content:
(Prior to the
commencement of this item, Councillors Greenway and Lury both
declared Personal Interests as Members of Bersted Parish
Council).
 
The committee
received a report from the Electoral Services Manager asking it to
approve the final timetable in place for conducting community
governance reviews across the district in preparation for the
creation of a unitary authority. The report also asked the
committee to agree to the formation of a Community Governance
Review Working Party and to agree its terms of reference for the
project. The working party would report into the committee to
progress the work that needed to be undertaken in line with the
timetable set out in Appendix 1 of the report.  
 
An update was also
provided in terms of the Town and Parish Councils that had
confirmed their wish for a CGR to be undertaken.
 
Before inviting
debate, the recommendations in the report were proposed by
Councillor Walsh and seconded by Councillor Butcher.
 
The chair asked the
Committee Manager to confirm the nominations put forward by Group
Leaders for the new working party. These were:
 
·      
Councillors Lury, Nash, Lawrence, Oppler.
·      
Councillor Gunner as Leader of the Conservative Group confirmed
that he would provide his membership outside of the meeting.
 
Concern was raised
over the formation of the working party and whether the
Constitution Working Party could absorb this work. The Assistant
Director for Governance, People & Performance responded
confirming that the Policy & Resources Committee held
responsibility for the functions of conducting community governance
reviews and electoral reviews which had transferred to it from the
former Corporate Support Committee as part of the review undertaken
of the committee system and so it was not possible for the
Constitution Working Party to undertake this work.
 
The Committee,
then
 
         
         
RESOLVED – that
 
(1)            
It approves the final timetable for the CGR programme as set out in
Appendix 1;
 
(2)            
It recommends to Full Council that the draft terms of reference for
the CGR programme as set out in Appendix 1 is approved;
 
(3)            
Approval is given to the creation of a CGR working party to
consider submitted representations to propose draft
recommendations.
topline: The Policy and Resources Committee has decided to approve the final timetable for conducting community governance reviews in preparation for the creation of a unitary authority.

purpose:
The Council has received a request from the
current operators of the Alexandra Theatre for financial support in
the lead up to and the early years of running the updated theatre.
This report considers the work that has been undertaken to explore
options for the operation of the theatre, soft market testing for
potential alternative operators and the request for support from
Arun Arts (the current operator). The recommendations endorse
providing the requested financial support for a three-year
period.
content:
The committee received a
report from the Deputy Chief Executive providing an update on the
support requested by the current theatre operator of the Alexandra
Theatre to enable the recommencement of theatre operations when the
theatre would reopen following the current investment programme of
works. A degree of financial support had been requested during the
early years of the new theatre’s operation and as it was
noted that investment in the theatre meant that the operator would
need to offer a wider range of facilities and an improved and wider
service compared to previous provision.
 
Members’ attention was directed towards an options
appraisal within the report which outlined work that had been
undertaken to soft market test for potential alternative operators,
and it detailed the request for support from Arun Arts. The
recommendations endorsed providing the requested financial support
over a three-year period.
 
         
The Deputy Chief Executive worked through the response that had
been received to that exercise.
 
The
recommendations in the report were then proposed by Councillor Lury
and were seconded by Councillor Nash.
 
The
chair then invited debate which saw a range of questions from
members which were responded to at the meeting.
 
As
part of those discussions, Councillor Nash, as seconder to the
recommendations, proposed an amendment to recommendation 4 to read
as set out below:
 
That
the Group Head of Technical Services and the Director of Resources
& Section 151 Officer be delegated to agree the final wording
of financial support conditions and the lease Heads of Terms in
accordance with any legal and procurement advice provided.
However, the preference is for Year 0 financing of Arun Arts
(£250,000) to be in the form of a grant, subject to further
appropriate legal and financial advice
 
This
amendment was seconded by Councillor Haywood.
 
Before proceeding further, the chair confirmed that in line with
Part 5, Section 2, paragraph 8 of the Constitution, the meeting
would need to conclude at 9.00 pm, unless a majority of Councillors
present voted to extend the meeting by 30 minutes.
 
The
chair therefore proposed to extend the meeting by 30 minutes after
9pm, and this was seconded by Councillor Nash. On this being put to
the vote it was declared CARRIED.
 
The
chair invited debate on this amendment. Having fully discussed it
and having put this to the vote, it was declared
CARRIED.
 
The
chair then returned to the substantive recommendations.
 
Following further extensive debate,
 
The
committee
 
         
         
RECOMMENDS TO FULL COUNCIL - That
 
1.    
Up to £50k in 25/26 to facilitate technical support during
the construction phase.
 
2.    
To provide financial support to the operators of the Alexandra
Theatre in the following three years as follows subject to
conditions.
 
YEAR 0 (Apr 26 – Mar 27)
£250,000.00
YEAR 1 (Apr 27 – Mar 28)
£170,000.00
YEAR 2 (Apr 28 – Mar 29)
£140,000.00
 
3.    
That the council enters into a new lease with Arun Arts for the
operation of the theatre based on the draft Heads of Terms set out
in this report; and
 
4.    
That the Group Head of Technical Services and the Director of
Resources & Section 151 Officer be delegated to agree the final
wording of financial support conditions and the lease Heads of
Terms in accordance with any legal and procurement advice provided.
However, the preference is for Year 0 financing of Arun Arts
(£250,000) to be in the form of a grant, subject to further
appropriate legal and financial advice.
topline: The Policy and Resources Committee has decided to provide financial support and enter into a new lease agreement with Arun Arts for the operation of the Alexandra Theatre.

In debating the

this was dealt with in administering the scheme and what checks and
balances were undertaken with applicants to limit fraud. Members
were informed that detailed questions were asked and evidence
requested from applicants to assess and ascertain suitability. The
other question asked was whether the council held any data on how
long people received the discount for, did the scheme have time
limits in place to ensure that recipients did not receive the
discount indefinitely and if this was not the case, could time
limits for claimants be considered.
 
The Director of
Resources confirmed that the council could not eradicate fraud but
that it did take steps to prevent it. The council had recently
launched a fraud referral service which had already uncovered one
example whereby a claimant was claiming housing benefit and the
local council tax reduction scheme whilst out of the country. This
hopefully provided members with a degree of comfort that the
council was doing its best to combat fraud.
 
The committee
 
RECOMMEND TO FULL
COUNCIL
 
That the Council
Tax Reduction Scheme for 2026/27 be implemented at a cost of
£30,548 per annum.

purpose:
An Infrastructure Funding Statement (IFS) is a
public report that summarises how developer contributions,
including those from the Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) and
Section 106 planning obligations, are used for infrastructure
projects. The report provides transparency for the Committee on how
funds are received, allocated, and spent, as well as outlining
future infrastructure priorities. This information must be
published each calendar year under the CIL Regulations 2010 (as
amended).
content:
The Chair invited
the Planning Policy & Conservation Team Leader to present the
report to the Committee.  The annual
Infrastructure Funding Statement provided an overview of Community
Infrastructure Levy (CIL) and Section 106 income and expenditure
for the previous financial year. Officers reported that £6.7
million had been received, comprising £2.9 million from
Section 106 agreements and £3.8 million from CIL receipts,
which represented a significant increase on previous years. A total
of 18 new agreements had been signed, delivering approximately
£1 million in contributions and non-monetary obligations, and
that 401 affordable homes had been provided. It was confirmed that
£6.57 million in Section 106 funds remained held and that CIL
receipts since 2020 totalled £4.4 million in demand notices
and £3.8 million received. Future spending priorities were
set out in the Infrastructure Investment Plan and processes for
spend would be reviewed to improve efficiency. The recent
appointment of a new CIL Assessment, Spend and
Monitoring Officer would support parishes.  There were plans to publish a separate report next
year showcasing projects delivered through these funding
streams.
 
         
The recommendation was proposed by Councillor Penycate and seconded
by Councillor Lury.
 
         
The Chair invited questions and comments from members: 

·      
A member asked what the expected timescale was for parish and town
councils to spend CIL and Section 106 funds.  The Planning Policy and Conservation Team
Leader advised that guidance required funds to be spent within five
years of receipt, with clawback provisions if unspent. Measures
were being introduced to encourage timely use, including spending
strategies for longer-term projects, which were expected to be in
place by the end of the financial year.

·      
Officers confirmed that updated guidance and contact details for
the new CIL Assessment, Spend and Monitoring
Officer had been circulated to all parish councils.

·      
A member suggested that the council should do more to inform the
public about developer contributions towards infrastructure, noting
that the link between housing development and infrastructure
improvements was often unclear. It was proposed that officers
explore ways to improve public awareness, including highlighting
delays caused by some of the delivery partners such as the NHS,
which were outside the council’s control.  The Planning Policy and Conservation Team Leader
confirmed that improved communication was planned, citing examples
from the South Downs National Park Authority and other councils
where branding and signage highlighted infrastructure funded by
development contributions.

·      
A member requested a list of Section 106 and CIL contributions
allocated to the Health Authority and their intended use. The
Planning Policy and Conservation Team Leader responded that in
terms of CIL funding, whilst not specifically allocated to
healthcare funding the Health Authority could bid for funding from
this pot.  He advised that recent
discussions had taken place with the Health Authority with regards
to future need and spend, and it was expected that they would
submit a case to support their requirements in the near
future.   Information relating to
specific Section 106 funds linked to specific development could be
provided to members and he undertook to provide this
information.   

·      
Members welcomed ongoing engagement with parishes and the
appointment of a new officer to support spending strategies. A
non-member was invited to address the Committee, who noted that a
useful spreadsheet listing unallocated Section 106 funds was
available on the council’s website.
 
The Committee
 
RESOLVED that:
 
The Arun
Infrastructure Funding Statement 2024/25 be noted and published on
the Arun District Council website, in accordance with Regulation
121A of the Community Infrastructure Regulations 2010 (as
amended).
topline: The Planning Policy Committee has decided to note and publish the Arun Infrastructure Funding Statement for the previous financial year.

content:
(Ahead of
commencing this item, the Chair called a short adjournment from
19.42 to 19.50).
 
         
The Chair confirmed
that one motion had been submitted for this meeting.
 
         
The Chair invited the proposer of the motion, Councillor Mrs Worne,
to present her motion.
 
         
Councillor Worne provided background to her motion, explaining that
it was prompted by an incident within her ward during the summer
involving a resident whose unreasonable actions caused significant
distress and disruption to other residents. She advised that the
matter had been challenging to resolve and, following discussions
with council officers, steps were taken to alleviate the situation.
During these discussions, questions were raised as to why a Fixed
Penalty Notice (FPN) could not be issued. It was confirmed that the
current procedure did not allow for this approach, requiring
enforcement through prosecution and, ultimately, court proceedings.
Councillor Worne stated that she had therefore undertaken
considerable research into how changes could be introduced to
enable the use of FPNs in similar circumstances, as a more
efficient alternative to the existing enforcement
process.
 
         
Councillor Worne expressed her appreciation to Councillors Lury and
Gunner for enabling her to present this cross-party motion,
highlighting it as an example of how political groups could work
collaboratively in the interests of residents.
 
To
assist Members in understanding the Council’s current
approach to such regulatory matters, a background paper had been
circulated. This confirmed that, within several regimes, such as
food safety, health and safety, alcohol licensing, taxi licensing,
mobile homes, and environmental protection, there was no option to
issue FPNs, with prosecution remaining the primary route for
addressing non-compliance.
 
FPNs
were a valuable regulatory tool, allowing matters to be dealt with
efficiently by offering an offender the opportunity to discharge
liability for conviction through payment of a fixed penalty.
Existing FPNs covered offences such as littering, fly-tipping,
other waste-related offences, and dog fouling. The background note
included a table listing the types of FPNs that could be issued and
the maximum penalty amounts. Councillor Worne further explained
that prosecutions were typically resource-intensive and resulted in
a significant time lag between the offence and court determination.
Also, fines and costs awarded upon conviction were often
insufficient to act as a meaningful deterrent and this needed to
change.
 
 
 
 
 
          It
was highlighted that, while FPNs were available in Scotland for
certain offences, such as breaches of an abatement notice under the
Environmental Protection Act 1990, they were not currently
available in England. The Council’s most recent prosecution
for such a breach resulted in a successful conviction, with a fine
of £1,000 and a contribution to the Council’s costs of
£2,160, against actual costs exceeding £13,000.
Significant resources could have been saved had FPNs been
available, as they would provide an essential intermediate
enforcement tool for managing nuisance.
 
In
addition to supporting more efficient and effective regulation, FPN
receipts would, in most cases, be retained by the Council and
reinvested in regulatory activities, including preventative and
educational initiatives, enhanced monitoring, and additional
inspections.
 
Councillor Worne confirmed that her motion sought to reduce
officer time and generate additional income. She expressed her
thanks to Councillor Greenway for seconding the motion and for his
collaboration in its development.
 
Councillor Worne then read out her motion which was asking the
council to:
 
The
council recognises the importance of our role in regulating a wide
range of matters to ensure the safety and wellbeing of Arun’s
residents.
 
This
council recognises the importance of effective, proportionate
enforcement to uphold local standards and protect the wellbeing of
Arun’s residents.
 
The
council therefore asks that the Deputy Chief Executive write to the
Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government to
request that the Government:
 
1. Extend the use of FPNs to
all district council regulatory areas where they are currently
unavailable, including environmental protection, housing standards,
and local licensing enforcement;
 
2. Allow district councils to
set FPN levels locally (within nationally prescribed limits), with
provision for discounted early payment;
 
3. Introduce escalating
penalties for repeat offences, ensuring proportionate deterrence
while reducing the need for formal court action, for example
doubling at each subsequent breach up to a maximum level;
and
 
4. Permit district councils to
retain all FPN income, ring-fenced for reinvestment in local
regulatory and enforcement activities.
 
Furthermore, this
council:
 
5. Commits to reviewing and
increasing the value of FPNs within its existing powers, to ensure
penalties act as a strong deterrent and demonstrate this
council’s determination to crack down on offences such as
fly-tipping, littering, and environmental damage. 
 
The
motion was then seconded by Councillor Greenway. 
 
The
Chair then invited debate which saw overwhelming support with
councillors confirming that it was well thought out; provided an
extremely compelling case; and carried a lot of weight. It was felt
to be something that needed to be developed ahead of LGR. It was
felt that it emphasised the need for improved reporting on FPNs,
moving beyond total numbers issued to include a detailed breakdown
by category and reason. This level of reporting would enable the
identification of trends and associated costs, providing valuable
insight for future decision-making. It was felt important to
highlight the importance of additional work behind the scenes to
ensure the reporting framework delivered maximum value going
forward.
 
Debate continued with councillors examining the rationale for
supporting the letter to be sent to Government which would seek
authority to apply the relevant legislation. There was concern that
many of the issues that the council encountered had progressed well
beyond the scope of a FPN with such cases generating significant
costs. Some key considerations were highlighted if approval to move
forward as the motion proposed was granted. There was concern over
what the financial implications might be as pursuing fines would
involve additional expenditure, including administrative and
recovery costs. The increased operational costs could place
pressure on existing budgets. Staff would require appropriate
training to ensure compliance and enforcement standards would be
met. A change in working conditions would need to be considered as
staff would need to work anti-social hours to deliver the service
effectively. It was acknowledged that any fines imposed should
reflect the substantial costs associated with running enforcement
teams These complexities and resource implications were likely
reasons why this matter had previously been overlooked. The
importance of proceeding with the full awareness of the potential
impact on budgets and staffing was highlighted by one
councillor.
 
Debate then expanded looking at the varying areas that could be
covered by FPNs. Coupled with this, councillors reflected upon the
difference enforcement had made to varying areas in the district in
the past and so they felt positive about reinforcing these
measures.
 
Councillor Greenway, as seconder of the motion, emphasised that
this marked the start of an important enforcement initiative. Since
April 2024, enforcement activity had been minimal, undermining
standards expected by residents. The council needed to ensure FPN
activities were current, effective, and fair to deter repeat
offences. Residents expected visible enforcement and so a strong
message needed to be sent that the council took enforcement
seriously. Councillor Greenway welcomed the cross-party
collaboration to address these long-standing public
concerns.
 
A
request was made to amend the motion slightly be removing the word
“district” from paragraphs 1, 2, and 4 of the motion.
This was agreed by the proposer, Councillor Worne.
 
An
additional request was made that the council should write to other
district and borough councils encouraging them to forward this
motion to their meetings. The Chief Executive confirmed this could
be easily actioned without the need for a further
amendment.
 
Councillor Worne, as proposer of the motion, expressed
appreciation for the strong support received from fellow
councillors. She highlighted that, with (LGR) approaching, it was
essential to address these issues to ensure the council left a
positive legacy by strengthening these services. Councillor Worne
emphasised the need for robust deterrents to prevent repeat
offenders from committing the offences previously
outlined.
 
The
council
 
         
         
RESOLVED – That
 
This
council recognises the importance of effective, proportionate
enforcement to uphold local standards and protect the wellbeing of
Arun’s residents.
 
The
council therefore asks that the Deputy Chief Executive write to the
Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government to
request that the Government:
 
1. Extend the use of FPNs to
all council regulatory areas where they are currently unavailable,
including environmental protection, housing standards, and local
licensing enforcement;
 
2. Allow councils to set FPN
levels locally (within nationally prescribed limits), with
provision for discounted early payment;
 
3. Introduce escalating
penalties for repeat offences, ensuring proportionate deterrence
while reducing the need for formal court action, for example
doubling at each subsequent breach up to a maximum level;
and
 
4. Permit councils to retain
all FPN income, ring-fenced for reinvestment in local regulatory
and enforcement activities.
 
Furthermore, this
council:
 
5. Commits to reviewing and
increasing the value of FPNs within its existing powers, to ensure
penalties act as a strong deterrent and demonstrate this
Council’s determination to crack down on offences such as
fly-tipping, littering, and environmental damage.
topline: The council has decided to request the government to extend the use of Fixed Penalty Notices to improve enforcement and regulation in Arun.
