content:
The Chair of the Policy & Resources Committee, Councillor Lury,
presented a recommendation following the meeting of the Policy
& Resources Committee held on 23 October 2025.
 
         
Councillor Lury referred Members to a recommendation at Minute 300
(Governance Reviews) which he duly proposed. The recommendation was
the seconded by Councillor Nash.
 
The Chair invited
debate. Speaking in support of the proposals, there were
councillors who felt strongly that all dual hatted councillors be
encouraged to engage in conversation with their parishes and
highlight the advantages of undertaking a community governance
review so that expressions of interest could be registered with the
council ahead of its deadline. 
 
          A
concern was raised by one councillor regarding unparished areas
regarding the inclusion of the unparished areas identified in the
table at paragraph 4.4 and the suggestion to explore the creation
of parish councils ahead of Local Government Reorganisation (LGR).
The councillor highlighted that these areas possessed a strong
sense of place and a long-standing, deeply rooted community
identity and history. There was apprehension that the proposals
could be perceived as an abolition of this identity. While
residents had been advised that the establishment of parish
councils might provide a stronger voice following LGR and
potentially confer greater powers and responsibilities, no detailed
information has been received from central government. This lack of
clarity and continued silence was causing significant concern, with
the perception that the proposals may be driven primarily by
bureaucratic simplification rather than community benefit.
 
Reassurance was
sought that any review would include confirmation of minor boundary
changes and that clear community preferences would be supported and
afforded significant weight. The councillor indicated that, should
these assurances not be provided, an amendment would be proposed to
remove the unparished areas identified in paragraph 4.4 from the
current proposals. Other councillors supported this view,
emphasising the need for further clarification on the implications
of this process for the unparished areas.
 
Councillors
expressed support for commencing a review of the unparished areas,
stressing the importance of this work in preparation for LGR. It
was noted that the review was essential to ensure appropriate
representation for these areas, particularly given the current
uncertainty regarding how the Government would address boundary
anomalies following LGR. Members agreed that progressing with the
review would enable comprehensive public engagement, ensuring
residents would be fully informed of the implications of the
changes.
 
In response,
Councillor Lury emphasised that this represented the commencement
of a comprehensive process to assess the potential establishment of
parish councils. This stage did not confirm that parish councils
would be created, nor did it imply that any other changes were
predetermined. The reviews would facilitate the identification of
any anomalies, which would subsequently be subject to public
consultation.
 
The Assistant
Director of Governance, People & Performance reminded
councillors that, in the context of LGR, principal authorities such
as Arun District Council had a statutory duty to ensure that an
appropriate democratic structure was in place across the district.
Parish boundary changes could be proposed by individual parishes,
and several parish councils had already expressed a clear interest
in being included within the Community Governance Review (CGR)
programme.
 
The Elections Team
had written to the councillor who had previously raised concerns
regarding unparished areas. It was acknowledged that the position
post-LGR remained uncertain, and the Council had shared its
concerns regarding the lack of clarity around parish arrangements.
However, at this stage of the LGR process, the Council had the
responsibility to review these areas, and now was the appropriate
time to undertake this work in advance of LGR, particularly in
those parts of the district that remained unparished.
 
Strong reassurance
was provided that a comprehensive public consultation process would
be carried out to seek views on future arrangements for these
areas. Full consideration would be given to all representations
received, and every effort would be made to ensure that all
residents would be engaged in the consultation process.
 
         
Following further debate, the Chair asked councillors to submit
their technical questions to the elections team so that full
responses could be provided. Ahead of voting on the recommendation
the council endorsed the approach in moving forward with the CGR
programme.
 
         
The Council
 
                   
RESOLVED
 
Having had the
committee considering and approving the proposal to carry out
community governance reviews for the Arun District in relation to
the areas provided in item 4 of the report, as well as any
subsequent requests received, the proposal be reported to Full
Council at its meeting on 12 November 2025.
 
(During the course
of the discussion on this item, Councillor Bence declared a
Personal Interest as a Member of Aldwick Parish Council).
topline: The Arun District Council has decided to move forward with community governance reviews, sparking concerns about potential abolition of community identity in unparished areas.

In the absence of
the Chair of the Licensing Committee, the Vice-Chair, Councillor
Haywood, presented the minutes from the meeting of the Licensing
Committee held on 12 September 2025.
 
         
Councillor Haywood alerted councillors to a recommendation at
Minute 225 (Renewal of the Statement of Licensing Policy) which she
formally recommended. The recommendation was then seconded by
Councillor Mrs Worne.
 
          In
debating the recommendation some questions were asked, and
clarification was sought on the role of the Licensing Committee as
the proposed changes outlined on pages 116–118 suggested that
responsibility for determining individual licensing applications
would transfer from the Licensing Committee to the Licensing
Sub-Committee. The Assistant Director of Governance, People &
Performance confirmed that this approach was common practice and
reflected good governance principles, as sub-committees could focus
on detailed casework, develop specialist knowledge through
training, and make decisions more efficiently. It was important for
councillors to note that the Licensing Committee would continue to
have a significant role. While application decisions would sit with
the Sub-Committee, the main Committee would retain responsibility
for broader functions. The delegation of functions proposed would
ensure that operational decisions would be handled by a smaller,
trained group, while the Licensing Committee maintained its
essential role in policy development and governance.
 
         
Having received the initial clarification, members sought further
explanation as to why the Licensing Committee should retain
responsibility for policy matters. It was queried whether these
responsibilities might more appropriately fall within the remit of
the Economy Committee or the Environment Committee, where other
licensing functions were considered. In response, the Assistant
Director of Governance, People & Performance advised that the
Licensing Act contained statutory provisions which required these
matters to remain within the Licensing Committee’s remit and
not be delegated to another committee such as the Economy
Committee. The Licensing Act 2003 placed a statutory obligation on
the Council itself to adopt the policy, rather than delegating this
responsibility to a committee.
 
Debate then turned
to the public consultation undertaken. Although it was acknowledged
that the response turnout had been small, it was noted that there
were several comments indicating a preference for premises to close
earlier at 10:30pm. The analysis referred to consideration of times
between 10 pm and 11 pm in residential areas, but did not appear to
address the consultation feedback suggesting an even earlier
closing time and had the committee considered this feedback?
Additionally, the officer response indicated that a separate time
for outdoor music could be considered. Was this option discussed by
the committee, and if not, could clarification covering the reasons
why be provided.
 
 
Councillor Haywood,
as proposer of the recommendation, expressed appreciation for the
valuable contributions made by councillors and reiterated the
Council’s statutory responsibility under the Licensing Act to
consider, agree, and publish a Licensing Policy. This requirement
was fulfilled by the Licensing Committee and subsequently brought
before Full Council in accordance with legislative provisions. The
Committee had undertaken a thorough review of the revised Statement
of Licensing Policy, which was presented with significant detail
and clarity. Councillor Haywood encouraged members to direct any
queries that they had to the Licensing Committee
 
         
The council
 
                   
RESOLVED
 
                   
That the revised Statement of Licensing Policy is adopted.
topline: The Licensing Committee has decided to adopt the revised Statement of Licensing Policy.

content:
Prior to inviting
the Assistant Director of People & Performance to present his
report, the Chair confirmed that once the committee had debated the
Q1 performance indicators, it would then consider the
recommendation submitted from the meeting of the Environment
Committee held on 18 September 2025 as it closely aligned to this
agenda item.
 
The Assistant
Director of Governance, People & Performance presented his
report, confirming that was his first time presenting the Quarter
One Key Performance Indicator (KPI) report, covering the period
from 1 April to 30 June 2025, following the senior management
restructure. Members’ attention was drawn to the change in
the presentation style from CP1 onwards as the KPIs were now
formatted in portrait style, with each Corporate Priority displayed
on a single page. It was hoped that this revised layout improved
readability for members.
 
Turning to the
recommendation for the Committee to consider from the Environment
Committee regarding the introduction of a new KPI focused on green
spaces, the Assistant Director of Governance, People &
Performance advised that should the committee agree in principle to
this proposal, the Group Head of Environment & Climate Change
would work with the contractor to develop a set of options. These
would be brought back to the committee, potentially in December,
for further consideration and selection of the preferred KPI. The
chosen KPI would then be referred to the Environment Committee for
final endorsement.
 
In concluding his
presentation, the Assistant Director of Governance, People &
Performance confirmed that he would happily respond to any
questions members might have on the report or the Environment
Committee’s recommendation.
 
Questions commenced
with the recommendation from the Environment Committee regarding
CP25 (Contractor achieving performance target for all green space
management operations following monitoring).
 
         
Councillor Greenway, as the proposer of the recommendation at the
meeting of the Environment Committee, confirmed that he required
clarification regarding the KPI colour coding for the Tivoli
contract. The reported score was 68%, which was above the target of
66. His understanding was that a score above target should be
marked green, whereas orange typically indicated performance within
15% of the target but not meeting it. He had become confused by the
reference to the 85–95% range at the bottom of the report,
which seemed to apply to both above and below target figures. He
asked if he could receive confirmation on how the colour coding was
being applied in this instance.
 
 
 
 
 
Additionally, he
raised a concern regarding how the KPI accounted for the size and
complexity of individual sites. For example, smaller sites such as
play areas required less resource and could be easier to maintain,
potentially resulting in higher scores. When aggregated, this could
skew the overall performance percentage. He suggested that the KPI
be reviewed to consider whether site size and complexity could be
weighted to ensure a more balanced and representative measure of
performance. Councillor Greenway confirmed that he had already
raised this with the Group Head of Environment & Climate
Change, via email, with it being confirmed that the points raised
would be responded to outside of this meeting.
 
In response, the
Assistant Director of Governance, People & Performance
acknowledged the points raised regarding the comparative challenges
between smaller and larger sites. He advised that this was a valid
observation that smaller sites could be more likely to achieve a
positive outcome, whereas larger sites could present greater
difficulties. It was confirmed that a written response would be
provided to the points raised which would be shared with all
members of the committee.
 
          A
range of questions were asked by the committee. These have been
summarised below:
 
·      
CP12 (Number of missed refuse and recycling collections per 100,000
within contractual target), in terms of the data received from the
contractor, what level of auditing was undertaken in terms of the
information received, was this checked? Could this question be
applied to other contracts and contractors. It was confirmed that a
written response would be provided.
·      
CP21 (% of emergency repairs completed within 20 working days)
– this target was set at 90%, yet performance in Quarter 1
stood at 65%, achieving a red rating. This was a matter that had
been raised on numerous occasions over the years, as repairs
continued to be a challenging area. Whilst it was acknowledged that
work was ongoing to address this, disappointment was expressed over
the current performance level. Reassurance that improvement was
underway was sought.
·      
CP24 (Household waste sent for reuse, recycling and composting)
– disappointment over what had been achieved was expressed.
The committee stated that this made it very difficult for it to
provide meaningful scrutiny due to the time lag in performance
reporting. The Chief Executive acknowledged this challenge,
confirming that this was unavoidable due to the structured cycle of
meetings. The Deputy Chief Executive confirmed that the lower
performance levels observed during the reporting period could be
attributed to an extended spell of dry weather, which significantly
reduced the volume of green waste generated, particularly grass
clippings. While collections continued as scheduled, the quantity
of material available for collection was notably diminished. This
reduction in volume directly influenced the percentages, not due to
operational inefficiencies, but simply because there was less green
waste to collect. As noted in the report, other recycling streams
performed largely as expected, indicating that the dip in
performance was specific to green waste and closely linked to
environmental conditions.
·      
CP43 (Overall tenant satisfaction) - how was this information
collected from tenants. It was confirmed that a written response
would be provided by the Assistant Director of Housing &
Wellbeing.
 
The committee then
returned to general debate and raised two process related concerns
in relation to the current KPI report, which it believed impacted
its ability to carry out effective scrutiny, this was the lack of
comparative quarterly data. As the report did not provide Q1
performance data from the previous year, this limited
members’ ability to assess progress or identify trends. This
had been a concern raised before. Were there any reasons why the Q1
performance figures from the previous year could not be included in
future reports as this would allow members to make meaningful
comparisons and assess whether performance had improved
year-on-year. Another concern raised was that the individual KPI
sheets were currently not presented in numerical order, which made
it difficult for members to locate and reference specific
indicators during meetings. It was suggested that the KPIs be
renumbered to reflect the grouped order for this committee, since
other committees only received their own KPIs. If this was not
possible, that an index or guide be produced to assist members in
navigating their way through the document.
 
The Chair agreed to
take the feedback on board. The Assistant Director of Governance,
People & Performance confirmed he would investigate cumulative
targets and the inclusion of Q1, Q2, or Q3 figures from the
previous year. A request was made that in addition to cumulative
figures, there were other KPIs with year-on-year variations. It
would be beneficial for the committee to see these changes across
the year. It was agreed that this comparative data would be
provided where possible.
 
Finally, the
proposal to develop a KPI for the Environment Committee relating to
street cleansing was welcomed and so the committee then turned its
attention to the recommendation for it to consider from the meeting
of the Environment Committee held on 18 September 2025. This
proposed that officers investigate creating a KPI for the
Environment Committee around street cleansing. The Assistant
Director of Governance, People & Performance confirmed that, if
this principle was accepted by the committee, the Group Head of
Environment & Climate Change would work with the contractor so
that a range of options could be presented to the Environment
Committee.
 
Before inviting
debate, Councillor Nash proposed the recommendations which were
seconded by Councillor Walsh.
 
         
Having received the full support of the committee, the
committee
 
                   
RESOLVED
 
That Officers look
at creating a KPI for the Environment Committee around street
cleansing.
topline: The Policy and Resources Committee has decided to create a Key Performance Indicator for the Environment Committee focused on street cleansing.

content:
The Chair invited
the Corporate Complaints Manager to present her report, the
recommendations within the report were then formally proposed by
Councillor Hayward and seconded by Councillor Walsh.
 
The Committee was
informed that it was being presented with two items, the first was
the Quarter One Corporate Complaints Performance Report which
provided a high-level summary of the council’s corporate
complaints performance, including compliance with the
Ombudsman’s Joint Complaint Handling Code. Members were
reminded that this item was previously reviewed by the Corporate
Support Committee.
 
The key points for
Members to note were highlighted, these included:
 

Stage One complaints performance in
June was just 1% below the target of 80%, indicating a marked
improvement since the start of the financial year.
Stage Two complaints were fewer in
number, meaning that even one or two late responses could
significantly impact the overall percentage.
The volume of complaints was lower
compared to the same period last year, although it was too early to
determine whether this trend would continue.
Housing repairs remained the most
frequent area of complaint, consistent with previous quarters.
There was one determination from the
Housing Ombudsman during Quarter One, and all associated orders and
recommendations had been fully complied with.
There were no determinations from
the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman during this
period.

 
         
Turning to the Updated Corporate Complaints Policy, the Corporate
Complaints Manager confirmed that the Committee’s approval of
the updated policy was sought. The existing policy, written in
2022, predated the introduction of the Joint Complaint Handling
Code.
 
Following a review
by the Housing Ombudsman’s compliance team, 26
recommendations had been made to bring the policy in line with the
new code. It was confirmed that all the new recommendations had
been incorporated into the updated policy.  Once approved by this Committee, the policy would
be resubmitted to the Housing Ombudsman along with a revised
self-assessment form for final approval.
 
In discussing the
report, concerns were raised regarding the timeliness of responses
to Stage Two complaints. This was because, although the number of
complaints was low, delays even by a day or two could significantly
impact performance results. The importance of resolving complaints
promptly to maintain public confidence and improve reported
outcomes was emphasised. The Corporate Complaints Manager
acknowledged the concern and explained that Stage Two complaints
were typically more complex and required thorough investigation.
While efforts were made to respond within target timescales,
pressures across different service areas could lead to delays.
 
It was noted that
performance was measured at the point of response, not receipt, and
that a high volume of complaints in one month could affect the
following month’s capacity to respond. This could result in
apparent performance drops, even when the number of complaints was
small. The Corporate Complaints Manager highlighted that agreed
extensions with complainants were sometimes not communicated
centrally, leading to inaccurate reporting. A cultural shift was
needed to ensure such agreements were logged and that complainants
were proactively informed of any delays.
 
A Councillor
queried the month-on-month drop in performance from May (green
rating) to June (red rating), despite fewer complaints in June. It
was explained that the timing of responses and internal pressures
could affect monthly outcomes. They also noted that some teams were
more affected than others and that improvements were being made to
standardise the use of ombudsman-approved extensions.
 
          In
conclusion, the committee acknowledged the complexities involved in
handling Stage Two complaints and the challenges of reporting
performance based on small numbers. Officers committed to improving
internal communication and complaint tracking processes with the
committee continuing to monitor performance and consider
alternative reporting methods where appropriate. Already, it was
positive to report that early indications suggested that this was
already having a positive impact. The Complaints manager reported
that nearing towards the Quarter 2 timelines, there was noticeable
improvement, which reflected the effectiveness of the changes
implemented. It was encouraging to see progress and that the
strengthened policy appeared to be contributing positively.
 
The Committee
 
RESOLVED – That
 
(1) 
The contents of the report be noted; and
 
(2)  
The Updated Corporate Complaints Policy is approved.
topline: The Policy and Resources Committee has decided to approve the Updated Corporate Complaints Policy.

content:
The committee
received the minutes from the meeting of the Housing &
Wellbeing Committee held on 11 September 2025.
 
The Chair drew
Members’ attention to a recommendation at Minute 247
[Disregard of Income from War Pensions and Armed Forces
Compensation Scheme for the Purpose of Assessing Housing
Benefit].
 
The Chair invited a
proposer and seconder. Councillor Pendleton formally proposed the
recommendation which was seconded by Councillor Walsh.
 
The Chair then
invited debate. This saw the committee expressing strong and
unanimous support for the ongoing initiative to support veterans
within the district. It was widely acknowledged that those who had
served deserved recognition and assistance, and that this
initiative represented a vital step in fulfilling that duty.
 
The
committee’s thanks were extended to Councillor Turner, in his
capacity as the council’s Armed Forces Champion, for his
commitment on behalf of veterans. His dedication was described as
invaluable, with several members noting his consistent efforts and
proactive approach.
 
Councillor Walsh,
as seconder to the recommendation, spoke as a former serviceman and
reservist, voicing his full support for the initiative, emphasising
the deep sense of gratitude owed to veterans. He encouraged parish
councils to actively identify and engage with veterans in their
communities to better understand and address their needs.
 
Councillor
Pendleton, as proposer of the recommendation, highlighted Arun
District Council’s commendable approach to veteran support,
particularly the inclusion of a question in council documentation
asking, “Have you served?” This practice, introduced by
the council’s safeguarding team was praised as a simple yet
effective way to identify veterans and tailor support accordingly.
Members were encouraged to adopt similar measures within their own
parishes.
 
Following further
discussion, the committee, having praised the council’s
collaborative efforts which were seen as being instrumental in
advancing veteran support across the district,
 
RESOLVED
 
That the
council supports our veterans by disregarding in
full any amounts above the statutory disregard for the purposes of
awarding housing benefit entitlement.
topline: The Policy and Resources Committee has decided to support veterans by disregarding income from War Pensions and Armed Forces Compensation Scheme for the purpose of awarding housing benefit entitlement.

content:
The committee
received a report from the Director of Resources and Section 151
Officer which was presented by the Revenues and Benefit Team
Manager (Recovery) seeking approval to write-off outstanding
business rate charges.
 
Under Part 7,
Section 2, Paragraph 1.2.10 of the council’s constitution,
the Director of Resources & Section 151 Officer had delegated
authority to write off irrecoverable business rates debts of up to
£30,000. Amounts greater than this required the approval of
the Policy & Resources Committee.
 
The report provided
the background detail and the extensive efforts made to recover the
debt highlighted. It was explained that the write-offs outlined in
the report could be funded within the budgeted bad debts provision
so there would be no direct impact on the council’s budget,
but future bad debt provision would need to be reviewed as part of
the 2026/27 budget setting process. However, it was strongly
emphasised that the council would seek to minimise the cost of
future write-offs by taking all appropriate action to recover what
was due. The council had since engaged the services of Oxford Fraud
Investigation Services so any future cases could be investigated
and prosecuted via this method. It was anticipated that this would
play a major role in mitigating the risk and impact of fraudulent
activity.
 
The recommendation
in the report was then proposed by Councillor Walsh and seconded by
Councillor Nash.
 
Following a full
debate,
 
The Committee
 
                   
RESOLVED
 
That the
outstanding charges set out with the report are authorised for
write-off.
 
(During the course
of the debate, Councillors Greenway, Pendleton and Walsh all
declared a Personal Interest in their capacity as Members of West
Sussex County Council).
topline: The Policy and Resources Committee has decided to approve the write-off of outstanding business rate charges exceeding £30,000.

purpose:
Sussex Chamber of Commerce has requested
membership of the Greater Brighton Economic Board. Extending the
membership of the Board triggers a variance in the Board’s
Heads of Terms that requires the formal ratification of all Joint
Committee members. Each member needs to individually ratify the
membership of proposed new members in accordance with their own
internal committee processes. In Arun’s case this means a
report to the Policy and Resources Committee.
content:
The Chair invited
the Business & Economy Manager to introduce the report. Before
opening the item for debate, the Chair sought a proposer and
seconder for the recommendations. Councillor Walsh proposed the
recommendations which were seconded by Councillor Nash.
 
The Chair then
invited members to debate or ask questions. A concern was raised
regarding the benefits of the Board’s activities to the
district with reference being made to previous discussions held
about the value of the Council’s membership. The Chair was
asked if he could provide assurance that the inclusion of the
Sussex Chamber of Commerce would enhance the Board’s
effectiveness and deliver meaningful outcomes for Arun.
 
In response, the
Chair cited the Department for Business and Trade’s recent
visit to a Littlehampton business, facilitated through the Board,
as evidence of the Board’s value. The Chair also noted the
strategic importance of developments at Shoreham Port. He confirmed
that he felt that the Sussex Chamber of Commerce would bring
valuable expertise and skills to the Board and that he viewed the
opportunity positively.
 
The Business &
Economy Manager then formally presented the report. She confirmed
that the Sussex Chamber of Commerce had applied for membership and
that the Committee’s approval was required. She also
explained the rationale for delegating future approvals to
streamline the process.
 
A request was made
that the two recommendations be voted on separately, the Chair
agreed to this request.
 
The Committee
 
         
         
RESOLVED – That
 
(1) 
It approves the Sussex Chamber of Commerce being
granted membership of the Greater Brighton Economic Board;
and
 
(2) 
Going forward, the Committee delegates authority to the Deputy
Chief Executive, in consultation with the Leader of the Council, to
approve the addition of new Members to the Greater Brighton
Economic Board.
topline: The Policy and Resources Committee has decided to approve the Sussex Chamber of Commerce for membership of the Greater Brighton Economic Board and delegate authority for future member approvals.
